response_text:
Dear City Council,

 

    I write to you today to express my concerns regarding the proposal to construct a new 18-hole golf course and clubhouse at the site of the existing public park. Although the continued economic success of the city is important to not just myself, other residents, and the elected council; I urge council to prioritize the voices of the majority of residents who oppose this project, and also consider the negative environmental impact that will result if this project moves forward. 

 

        Our voices matter. According to the 'Connecting Communities Poll', which asked city residents if they support replacing the public park with a golf course, a strong majority of residents aged 18-54 responded in opposition. I also believe it would be fair to say that those under 18 would prefer a park to a golf course if asked! The park is one of the few green spaces left for residents to enjoy, providing a free space for family gatherings, wellness activities, and for children to play. The park is a cornerstone of our community. 

 

    Residents and environmental groups have also expressed their concern on how this project would impact the environment and effect the many animals that call this park home. Families enjoy seeing birds and little critters around the park, it is an opportunity for children to experience and learn about nature. Environmental groups presented research on the potential environmental impacts that the golf course project could have. This research support the disruption of wildlife habitats but also notes that a golf course could lead to an increase demand for water usage. A demand for increased water usage could lead to unintended consequences such as water restrictions for residents and local businesses and increased tax dollars to account for the need for a larger water infrastructure. 

    Preserving our park is important to this community. Myself and the majority of residents who oppose this project trust that you will find the negative outcomes of this project outweigh the positives, and you will allow us to enjoy our park for generations to come.

 

Regards, 

Ryan Smith

Dear Management Team, 

 

I am writing to share my perspective on the recent proposal to implement a mandatory one-hour lunch break. This topic is important as schedule management directly affects staff wellness and their efficiency at work. After considering the proposal, I respectfully support this change, as employees benefit more than one hour of rest allocated for such a break. My position is based on employees' well-being, the needs for motivation and retention, and the overall work efficiency at the company. The following paragraphs explain why a mandatory one-hour lunch break is essential for our workplace. 

 

One key reason I agree with the implementation of a mandatory one-hour lunch break is staff wellness. Employees may enjoy more health benefits such as enough time for meals, increased everyday body movement, and improved relationships with colleagues. For example, an office employee who sits at their own desk most of the work hours can use the lunch break to stand up, stretch themselves, and chat with their colleagues. This can reduce work stress and potentially make their collaborations with coworkers smoother. Therefore, a mandatory one-hour lunch break improves the overall well-being of our staff.

 

Another important reason for my position is that such a mandatory one-hour lunch break is essential for employee motivation and retention. Satisfying employees with enough time to eat, rest, and interact with their colleagues in a lunch break are motivated because they see their employer genuinely care about their well-being and are more willing to work long-term for the company. For instance, warehouse workers may seek employment elsewhere where they find hard to feed themselves enough or rest well because of the limited lunch break time enforced by a company. This can increase turnover and eventually increase the recruitment and training costs for the company. Therefore, a mandatory one-hour lunch break boosts employee motivation and retention.

 

Some employees may argue such a mandatory one-hour lunch break will sacrifice company operations and reduce employees' ability to manage their own schedules. However, as I mentioned above, such a lunch break as a good refresh may improve the overall work efficiency, particularly for those hours in the afternoon. For example, employees may not feel fatigue or dizzy if they fully utilize the one-hour lunch break to eat healthy or maybe even take a nap. Moreover, employees have full control of their work schedules, as they have four hours before and the other four after the lunch break to focus on their work. Consequently, this counterargument is not strong enough to oppose the proposal.

 

In conclusion, I support the proposal to implement a mandatory one-hour lunch break at our workplace. The improvement in staff wellness, employee satisfaction, and work efficiency demonstrates why implementing a mandatory one-hour lunch break benefits the company. Thank you for considering this perspective as you make your decision.

 

Sincerely, 

John Doe

response_text:
To whom it may concern,

 

I have received the memo about the proposed policy to add a mandatory 18% tip to all customer bill. While this can be a new, exciting change for all, I disagree with this policy because it lowers our customer satisfaction, reduces our overall tips, and lowers our quality of service. These are the following reasons.

 

First, the policy to add an 18% mandatory tip to all customer bill will reduce customer satisfaction because customers like to have options. The purpose of a tip is to give customers a chance to show how much they loved the place and the person who served them, as well as a chance to feel good for helping someone out of their own, free will. Once we start forcing customers to tip, it is likely to leave a negative impression on the restaurant as a whole, since we will be taking that freedom away from them. This will also inevitably increase the number of frustrated customers during service, which will ruin the dining experience of our other guests. This will devalue the amazing food and service we provide, which can lead to lower ratings on review sites such as Google Maps or Yelp. This is important as happy customers are likely to become regulars, which can then bring more customers, thereby increasing our overall profit and tips, and if we leave a bad impression, they will be less likely to come back next time.

 

Second, this new policy will reduce our overall tips as customers who feel forced to tip will be less likely to become generous with them. When you force a child to do an errand, this will make the child upset and less likely to obey. When you ask them nicely, and treat them with kindness and respect, they will be more likely to comply. Our guests are no different. If we keep providing our amazing food and service, without asking for tips in return, they will be happier to tip, even more than 18%, as they get to show their appreciation while still being the one in charge. This is important because some customers are experiencing "tip fatigue" due to being forced to tip elsewhere, and if we can alleviate that by not having this policy, this is increase overall tip for the staff.

 

Third, this new policy will lower our quality of service. There are two reasons for this. The first reason is that staff members will be less likely to give effort to provide excellent service to our guest. Tips are essentially incentives for our customer facing team to be as welcoming, polite, and to go above and beyond for our guests, as there is a chance a guest will not tip if they are unhappy, or will provide a generous tip if they're happy. This policy will be taking that incentive away, as having a guaranteed tip will give our staff no reason to put as much effort as before. The second reason why this will lower our quality of service is because this will increase friction between our team and our guests. Guest who feel forced to tip will be more likely to become frustrated. Some frustrated guests are not afraid to cause a scene, in order for them to regain control. They are also harder to deal with for our staff, which can lead to burnout when it happens frequently due to this policy. As a result, our tired staff, without any incentive to provide excellent service, will inevitably reduce our capability to provide customers the level of excellence that we can give them. This will lead to lower profit for the company, and lower overall tips for everyone. 

 

To summarize, I disagree with this proposal because it lowers our customer satisfaction, reduces our overall tips, and lowers our quality of service. I sincerely hope that management will make the right decision when it comes to implementing this policy, and carefully consider the reasons I have provided. Thank you.

    Imagine, just for a second, that you're in a drive-thru at a Tim Hortons, and the attendant hands you the machine to pay, you dig through what seems like a mountain of cards, some that expired ages ago and some that still have the activation sticker on them to haphazardly hand one of them to pay for the $1.5 coffee you thought to treat yourself before coming into work, only for the machine to respond with an angry beep and the attendant softly saying "Sorry, your card has been declined". You dig through your wallet for remnants of coins because your bank is in overdraft and continue your trip to work. No one would be attuned to the fact of my struggles, team morale would be the least of my concerns when I'm thinking about where my next meal is going to come from.

 

    Freedom, a word that somehow seems elusive at best of times. Something that we all yearn for, freedom of speech, the freedom of choice and autonomy is important to the well-being of everyone. While it is only a $100, taking away a colleague's choice to decide for themselves is destructive to the autonomy that we all hold dear to heart.

 

    The division of the funds would also be tricky, because who gets to decide where the money goes? What if I don't like parties or coffee? It's hard enough deciding on a diner for us to go to on special occasions let alone trying to figure out how a large pool of funds should be distributed.

 

    Furthermore, looking at the survey results, it's hard to decipher as to when it was collected, did colleagues know that they'd have to contribute to the fund? Were they made to fill it out with onlookers watching? It's also important to be cognizant of the fact that it's not an overwhelming majority that is for the social fund. It seems like the older people get, the less they want it. This also doesn't seem to account for the fact that while 79% of the 18-24 age group has voted "Yes", we only have 2 in that demographic whereas the majority of our workforce is the older groups which seem to be against the fund.

 

While I do agree that having a social fund, and walking into an office that has the smell of fresh donuts and coffee whisking through the air would be heavenly on a cold morning, I think ultimately, taking away the autonomy from colleagues is a tricky proposition. 

 

Attributing to the essence of autonomy, the impossible nature of foresight into the financial well-being of our colleagues and the potential of the survey results to be skewed within context reaffirms my choice to decide against this movement to have a social fund. If it is still rolled out, I would suggest that we at-least have a segmented focus group to see how well it works before we scale it out to the rest of the workforce.

If we had not been dependent on one another, we would not have come as far as we have as a species. The fact that the farmers' market has been proposed to be held by the community centre speaks volumes to me. Although, when there are no incentives put in place, it is shockingly easy to get stuck as individuals in our own narratives. 

By having the farmers' market held every Saturday from 8:00am to 6:00pm, that provides a full ten hours weekly to interact with others and strengthen social ties that would not have otherwise existed. It promotes families with children having somewhere to take their kids out on the weekends, somewhere for couples of any age or duration to go on dates, somewhere for friends to gather and catch up. Hello City Council,

 

I'm writing this email in response to your proposal to hold a farmer's market every Saturday between the hours of 8:00 AM 6:00 PM, to which my opinion on this is that I wholeheartedly agree! A weekly get-together for people all over our community, which both supports human connection and healthier eating for all is absolutely worth losing the parking space for a few hours each week.

 

I've always been an advocate for healthy eating and paying attention to what your diet consists of. Alas, the grocery stores and markets I usually go to are quite busy on the weekends, which makes last-minute shopping or sudden cravings difficult when going out to get them becomes a hassle. The farmer's market at the nearby community centre is the solution to this problem! Not only does it provide a closer area for me, and several others, to go shopping for food on the weekends, but the food at farmer's markets are locally sourced and sustainably grown by honest farmers. This makes the food there generally better to eat than those found at large chain supermarkets that use pesticides and GMOs. The relative closeness of this market would also incentivize people to consider eating the healthier foods at the farmer's market as opposed to taking the longer trip for the less healthy items grown at supermarkets and grocery stores. As well, one source tells us, "these markets provide fresh, seasonal produce while helping reduce the carbon footprint tied to food transportation." Another reason why a farmer's market would be the better choice over typical chain grocery stores.

 

All this attention to healthy eating would also make a great subject for the community to bond over: an optional event every Saturday that allows people to get together, talk about their favourite foods, how they're grown, and economically support each other would be an excellent way to get people to connect. They say that the quickest way to a man's heart is through his stomach; I can personally attest to the truth of that idiom! Even from my own personal experiences, I've had the best times of my life connecting with friends and family over food, and I wholeheartedly believe that the same could apply for anyone who chooses to come visit our local farmer's market.

One source even claims, "Beyond food, farmer's markets support local artisans and small businesses by boosting the economy, bringing people together, and strengthening social ties." As you can see, there is research to back up my claims!

 

But, I cannot write an email expressing my interest without addressing the feelings of those who are opposed to the proposal for the farmer's market. In conclusion, even with these complaints and difficulties, I still agree with the proposal for a farmer's market to be held every Saturday at 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM. I am writing this email to you in regard to the newly proposed tipping policy here at Cozy Corner Bistro. I understand that this is a big change and hasn't been rolled out without careful consideration but with that being said, I do believe that it is worth having a conversation about it before it is finalized and implemented.

 

While I understand the sentiment behind the policy, I don't agree with the policy and I feel as though it could be improved. After reading your email to us, I did some research about the realities of "tip culture" and I came across an article called "Modern Workplace Trends" that really helped shape my opinion. One thing that the article highlighted was that there was still much uncertainty about the effect that a mandatory tip policy would have on employee's take-home pay. I found this interesting because the same sentiment was shared in our work group chat. An employee brought forward an idea that I would like to expand on. They said "If we're guaranteed a tip no matter how well we serve, some of us might not try as hard to give extra good service". I agree with them wholeheartedly, and I think this policy leaves the door open to be exploited by employees who may not be willing to earn their tips through outstanding service. I am quite sure that the other employees will take note of this and (understandably) become frustrated in the fact that their earnings are not in their full control anymore. This will cause friction between employees and demoralize the ones who work hard to bring in the largest sum of tips. I understand that the sentiment is based in equity and aims to make sure that each employee has an equal share of tips, but this doesn't take the point of what a tip is into consideration. A tip is a generous reward from the customer to the employee for outstanding service, and while it is a fair point to raise that employees should not be basing their service on the expectation of tips, ignoring that reality will only hinder the morale and performance of the employees.

 

We have yet to touch on the customer's perspective of this policy, the article I mentioned earlier also talked about how digital payment systems are prompting higher tip percentages which in turn is leading to what is called "tip fatigue" which is leading to lower overall gratuity levels. Going back to what a tip is, it is a gift for outstanding service, it should be treated as such and from a customer's perspective, it puts me into a position where I could be paying a large sum of additional money (because 18% is not a little amount) for service that I may not have even been happy with in the first place. It will raise the cost for the customer and put them in a position where they are forced to give extra money even for potentially sub-par service in the name of equity. If I were a customer, a mandatory tip policy may deter me from visiting any given store altogether, not because I don't like to tip, but because I have to.

 

I hope that I have made my stance clear, perhaps this email has provided management with another perspective to consider before the implementation of this new policy, I believe that we should leave the tips for our employees to earn and ensure that the customers are able to spend their money at their discretion, which I am quite sure they would appreciate.

Ghassan

To < Manager's Email Address >

Subject Re: URGENT Mandatory Tipping

 

Dear [Manager],

 

I've read your memo regarding mandatory tipping and would like to offer my thoughts on the proposal. I disagree that a mandatory 18% tip should be added to all customer bills at Cozy Corner Bistro because some customers tip more than 18%, it may result lessened motivation to do our best work, and some customers may be discouraged from dining at our restaurant at all.

 

First, some customers may wish to tip more than 18% when dining at Cozy Corner Bistro. My first attachment, the bar graph entitled "Tipping in Restaurants," clearly indicates that more than 33 in 100 people opt to tip at least 20% or more when dining out at a restaurant. By this logic, about one third of our patrons are likely to tip more than the mandatory 18% that is being proposed when they have the choice of what percentage to select. We must consider the fact that a mandatory 18% tip on all customer bills would also mean an 18% cap on all tips.

 

Next, implementing a flat 18% tip per table may lead to a sense of complacency or decreased job satisfaction amongst our most financially-motivated servers. In North America, the standard in our industry remains that, for better or worse, servers tend to be paid near minimum wage, which is then garnished by the amount of tips individually earned per table served. Under this current system, delivering excellent customer service makes it likelier that the received in tips will increase, but what happens when our servers know that delivering either "good" or "bad" service will yield the same results? Those primarily motivated by the amount of tips they can bring in per table may suffer a decrease in job satisfaction that may result in a lower expenditure of effort per table, or even seeking out alternative employment wherein tips are, once again, more reciprocal to the quality of service provided.

 

Finally, and most worrisome, instituting a mandatory 18% tip may discourage some customers from dining at Cozy Corner Bistro at all. My second attachment includes an excerpt from an article titled "Modern Workplace Trends," which discusses the newer phenomenon of "tip fatigue." As customers are prompted to tip higher percentages at more retailers than they ever have been before, some are experiencing a sense of frustration with regard to the prevalence of these additional expenses. In addition, the bar graph we looked at earlier indicates that a mandatory tip of 18% is greater than what the average customer is likely to pay when they choose to tip themselves. Forcing our customers to tip every time they come to Cozy Corner Bistro at a rate that is higher than average may frustrate some customers and be more than others can afford.

 

In summary, we should not institute a mandatory 18% tip on all customer bills because some customers would like to tip higher, it may lessen financial motivation to perform at our best, and we may lose some of our clientele due to this additional expense.

 

Best,
Azra Nezirovic

My name is Ricardo Vasquez, and I'm employed as one of your servers. I'm writing in regard to the staff memo about charging customers a mandatory 18% tip and after considering the information and opinions from various sources I respectfully disagree with the mandatory 18% tip that will be enforced.  

My reasons are as follows: 
It's unfair to the customers;
First and foremost, it is unfair to the customers to be forced to tip, let alone a specific percentage.  They should have the choice to tip if they want to, and if they see the value. The level of service they get should determine how much they would like to tip. I don't think it is right to force someone to tip if they don't want to or don't even have the ability to. Not everyone does. Poor service; 
I believe that if you guarantee a mandatory tip amount to all servers the quality of the service will suffer. The incentive is gone. There is no need to go above and beyond to earn the tip because you're guaranteed to get a specific percentage. That will lower their motivation to add more value. That will eventually create a poor experience for the customer. Overtime, that's fewer customers returning to your restaurant. Good servers will leave 
If a server isn't being rewarded for the value they are adding, they'll just go to a restaurant that does. I believe people will not tip more than they're being forced to.  I know that I personally wouldn't tip above what is being enforced.  Unfair to the best servers
If you pay 2 servers the exact same regardless of the value each of them bring, this is unfair. You're essentially punishing the server who has the greater skill set under the guise of "fairness" when that in and of itself is unfair. If they have exceptional rapport building skills, better memory, a more attractive personality, and provide an overall greater experience for the customers then they should have the chance to be rewarded as the customers see fit. Best regards, 

Ricardo Vasquez

Subject: Re: New mandatory 18% gratuity proposal

  Good day management team of Cozy Corner Bistro. As this proposal is aiming to go into effect next week, I am writing to you today to firmly express my opposition to this proposal.

   Management is considering a new policy to have an 18% tip added to all customer bills. Some in favour of the proposal believe it will ensure fair and stable earnings, however, it is my firm belief that this policy will; reduce earnings for higher performers, promote a poorer work ethic, and reduce the number of patrons to our establishment.

  A recent study by MgGill University (2024) showed that when customers are faced with a mandatory gratuity, they will choose that number regardless of the quality of service a staggering 80% of the time. This would greatly hurt higher performers as it would negate the entire concept of a gratuity, and when these higher performers can achieve tips ranging from 20%-30%, those losses can be quite significant and deter great staff from wanting to work at our establishment. Modern workplace-trends also show that digital payment systems are promoting higher tipping percentages when mandatory gratuities are not in place. 

  Furthermore, a study from The Fraser Institute (2023) showed that when staff are guaranteed a gratuity, quality of work often goes down. The study included 25 restaurants in the Vancouver area who had all implemented some form of mandatory gratuity and found that the restaurants averaged a 20% decrease in productivity (based on customer feedback, self-reports, and reviews by restaurant critics) which offset any benefit from the policies and saw 20 of the 25 restaurants drop those policies the following year.

   In addition to the above stated reasons, a Gallup Poll (2025) showed that auto gratuities are contributing to customer "Tip-Fatigue", which can affect overall gratuity levels and customers desire to frequent said establishment. The poll showed that 30% of customers felt "turned off" by the Auto-Gratuity, tipped less than they originally planned, and were less inclined to return even if the quality of their meal had been above satisfactory.

  In closing, to address the concerns of the people who are in favour of this policy proposal for the reasons of ensuring fair and stable earnings, we could implement higher base wages, but it is my firm belief that a mandatory gratuity would be detrimental not only to the staff, but to the restaurant itself. It would hurt higher performers, making them less likely to perform at their best and also detract them from wanting to work at this restaurant. It would promote poorer work-ethic overall as staff would not be encouraged to try harder. It would reduce the number of people wanting to eat at our restaurant out of "Tip Fatigue". For these reasons, I hope you will consider not implementing this policy, but rather make other adjustments to worker income and job satisfaction. 

  Sincerely, Jose-Luis Pino

Dear management,

 

    Hello! I've been a valued employee at JAM Mobile Applications for several years now, and the new manager's most recent announcement was that they want to introduce work uniforms. Unfortunately this is one of those ideas that sounds good on paper but never ends well, and will only result in resentment from both the employees and customers down the line.

 

    At JAM Mobile Applications, our job is to make video games for mobile devices. I've written the plot lines for three different video games JAM Mobile Applications has created, and as a result of everyone's creative spirit we've been able to produce high quality products every time! Individuality is of the utmost importance to keep that creativity; if we had uniforms there would be no such thing as individuality. As a result the office would feel less like a combined living space where everyone gets to relax while working on what they love, and instead like another sterile location in order to produce a product.     I know that JAM Mobile Applications values its employees as much as it values its products and customers. Whether they be from an administrator, manager, contractor or custodian; everyone can contribute to world design, dialogue, or a small plot point. Creativity is important; and individuality is one of the key factors that keep us creative. Uniforms would only stifle that creativity that everyone knows and loves.

 

    Sincerely,

    JAM Mobile Applications

To the Ring Road community at City Council,

 

Thank you all for providing the details that allowed us to better understand how may the Ring Road be developed and implemented, I truly appreciated your time and effort in trying to provide us a better living environment.

 

After reading comments shared by concerned citizens, meeting minutes, data supported graphics, and a virtual map, I'd like to express my thoughts about why I AGREE that this will be a great project to proceed with, from the perspective of Environment, Economy, and Living Experience.

 

Environment Perspective

The current congestion this city is experiencing daily, is leading towards a larger greenhouse gas pollution, and spiking up the Air-Pollution Index, causing more extreme weathers over the past few years.

 

Within the past 12 years, the air pollution index for average daytime carbon monoxide (CO) levels within city limits, has spiked up over 200%, from 25ppm to 60ppm. 

 

Our city had a huge population jump within those 12 years, so did the vehicle counts. We now have more motor vehicles stuck on the road daily, not to mention during morning and afternoon rush hours. I live right next to our school, and work at the recreation centre, my daily commute is now 35 mins driving my own vehicle, 50 mins on a bus.

 

When a motor vehicle is idling on the street, it releases more carbon monoxide, along with other polluted air than when it's driving. The longer the idle, the more polluted air was produced while we are waiting for a light.

 

The Ring Road will allow vehicle to take it as a connection road to the city highway, or an express way to other parts of the town without going through residential and crowded streets in the city. Each exits of the Ring Road will allow not only private vehicles, but also public transportation lines to reach different community in a more efficient way. 

 

The faster you can get there, the less gas we would have to burn while just sitting in the car doing nothing. Plus, the more efficient public transportation is, the less would our citizens use private vehicles, an extra bonus in cutting down air pollution!

 

Economy Perspective

As I previously mentioned, we were once a very small town, with limited population, so all of our facilities, entertainment, and community are all enclosing to the centre of this town, towards the Main Street.

 

While that was a great idea back in the days, not so much any more. With more people living outside of downtown, they will still need to come in downtown for both business, recreation, essential, or religious purposes, and that's making downtown to started to be overpriced (Like $8 for a regular coffee!), and overcrowded (how can you find parking in the city, on a Saturday night around the movie theatre?).

 

Roads brings in businesses as well. If the Ring Road gets approved, business development area would be a huge opportunity to boost our economy, bringing more jobs to the city (we already have a bad enough labour market), extra property, sales and income taxes. 

 

And these are just internal money flow we are speaking of. With better traffic system established, potential residents of this city, or people who live in the satellite cities, will be more willing to move, or travel here for entertainment, shopping, and doing businesses, or even develop more real estate business outside the Ring Road.

 

Despite most of the funding for this program will come from the provincial government as grants, most of them could be made back from the tax income, this will only be a positive cycle. There is a saying, "If you want development, build those road and bridges!"

 

Living Experience

At the moment, the Main Road is acting as the highway of our city, connecting to the intercity highway, which means sometimes, there will be people driving extremely fast, causing safety issues to themselves, others, and public properties.

 

The Ring Road will also provide more windows for residents who live outside the city, with more options. If you want to come to Church on Sunday morning at 10am? Leave at 9:40am, instead of 8:45am. If you want to be at your friends house across the city, drive for 15 mins instead of 45mins!

 

Other than the connection with human beings, some of us, including myself, love to throw myself into the nature and recharge. If the Ring Road would be implemented, driving from my house to the Wetlands Conservation Park will take only 10 mins, incredibly convenient!

 

According to the proposed map, our Fire Department will have a direct route to the Ring Road, providing residents with more assurance of their safety, if any unfortunate incident had happened, the firefighters would be able to be response and onsite faster than ever.

 

 

I understand that there are many voices within and outside the city council regarding this proposed project. As a citizen of this lovely place, I'm more than proud and happy to see that the council had gone over several versions of this proposal, trying to fit as many residents' needs as possible.

 

The progress of a city require changes, and I kindly ask our fellow citizens not to be feared by that, the core and culture of a city isn't about the new roads, buildings and infrastructure, is about how the people. Building a safer, greener and more developed community is absolutely the best way to go.

 

I'm very looking forward to see any further updates about the proposal of the Ring Road, or better news about when the work will begin :)

 

Thank you for taking the time to read my email, and I appreciate any feedback or response that your council may have regarding this email.

 

Kindest Regards,

 

Karen Wu, a concerned citizen

This decision must be viewed in the broader context of this generation planting a tree that we may never see to grow big!

    3- This is less of a policy or proposal concern but more of an "image" issue. The people who buy the products are also painted broadly with the same brush as being far left or right leaning. They can tend to be viewed as a wealthy clique.                                                                         Enthusiastic Constituent

We collectively believe that building an 18-hole golf course and clubhouse in the place of our beloved Forest Heights Park will drastically limit the availability of beautiful green spaces in our city, will create greater economic disparity between our citizens, and will be detrimental to the environment and our health.

 

    First, should this proposal be implemented, our city would lose yet another green space. Between Queen's Park being converted into new high-rise apartments last year, and the recent demolition of West Street Park to create a skate park, our community's number of green spaces have be dwindling rapidly. Forest Heights Park has always been a place where families gather for Sunday afternoon picnics, where children play after school, where dog owners walk their daily route, and where the elderly enjoy leisurely walks among the gardens. Personally, I have fond memories of playing catch there with my brother as children. To replace this park with yet another expensive golf course, would be replacing a beloved community gathering space for a money-making machine. This golf course would remove one of the last playgrounds, one of the last scenic ponds, and one of the last glimpses of beauty within our city. While our City Council has been focusing on what brings in the most revenue with tourism, critics like myself have been concerned about the wellbeing of our citizens. Forest Heights Park a cornerstone of this city's society, its beauty, and its wellbeing. Removing this cornerstone would be unequivocally detrimental.

 

    Next, the replacement of Forest Heights Park would increase the economic disparity within our community. The poll your council released concerning age groups in favour of the proposal supports this notion: 75 percent of those aged 24 and under, and 65 percent of the population under the age of 39 are opposed to the replacement. In fact, the only majority in favour is among those aged 55 and above. It is evident that young citizens are opposed to this proposal, because most people under the age of 55 cannot afford the high expenses required to participate in golf. Furthermore, these young citizens realize that this golf course would be eliminating one of the last free public recreation spaces. Where else do citizens have to go? If this policy is green-lighted, students, children, and the working class of the neighbourhood will be stripped of their free recreation, while rich senior citizens will be able to enjoy their leisurely afternoons golfing without a care in the world—or for those around them. For the younger population, quality of life will undoubtedly be reduced with the inaccessibility of recreation, while the older population will benefit off their misery. Forest Heights Park has always been an accessible park for all, allowing a variety of recreation for the entire city to enjoy. This golf course would be severely limiting, both financially and accessibility-wise.

 

    Finally, replacing our community park with an 18-hole golf course will negatively impact the environment through the overuse of water and pesticides, thereby impacting wildlife and humans alike. As a nearby resident of Forest Heights Park, I do not wish to be put at risk for such illnesses. Moreover, the wildlife that calls Forest Heights Park home would be affected as well. Every day I see Canadian geese, ducks, and plenty of beneficial pollinators in the park. With their environment removed, their water sources emptied, and exposure to pesticides, these animals would be harmed at the cost of raking in more money, and one more golf course this city does not need.

 

    It is for these reasons that I, along with most residents of this community, do not support the removal of Forest Heights Park to create an 18-hole golf course and clubhouse. I sincerely hope your council realizes the detriments this replacement will cause, and be able to see past the dollar signs in your eyes in order to think compassionately for your citizens.

Subject: Mandatory Tipping 

Dear Management,

    Cozy Corner Bistro needs to strongly reconsider introducing a mandatory 18% tip. While some restaurants have implemented similar tip policies, a mandatory 18% at a bistro is inappropriate. Management must also consider customers viewing mandatory tipping as dishonest or greedy, as tipping is generally considered optional in cafes and bistros. To avoid confusion and frustration  the term "mandatory tip" should be avoided, 18% should be lowered, and alternative methods of income stability should be considered.

 

    To maintain a positive public standing and avoid any possible legal issues, a different term should be used. Many restaurants have a mandatory gratuity fee that is the same as the proposed mandatory tip policy. By having a separate fee as opposed to mandatory tip the digital payment system can still prompt for a optional service based tip. This would also allow customers to decline to tip if they did not feel the service was adequate.

 

    A mandatory tip of 18% is far too high for a bistro. Data shows most people tip between 10%-15% at restaurants. If the base tip rate is too high customers may expect a much higher level of service than a bistro can provide. Many restaurants have found success by adjusting the tip prompts instead of outright forcing a tip. If Cozy Corner Bistro is to set a mandatory tip it should be based on the low side of the average customer tip, having the tip policy set too high could result in loss of return customers.

 

    There better customer friendly methods of increasing and stabilizing worker income that doesn't rely on  questionable tip policies. The simplest tactic commonly used is to adjust the tip prompt to be higher, or add a prompt if the digital payment system doesn't have one yet. Digital payment machines generally allow for 3 preset values and a custom. Using the 3 most common tip amounts of 10%, 15%, and 20% would likely help with tip stability. Alternatively adopting a no tip policy and increasing prices by 18% would be considered far more honest from a customer perspective.

 

    It is commendable of management to introduce a mandatory tipping policy, however it is likely inappropriate for Cozy Corner Bistro. Mandatory tipping is generally frowned upon in bistro and cafe settings and 18% is above the average tip amount. The proposed mandatory tip would likely be met with criticism due not only to the high rate but also the perceived dishonesty and greed. Many restaurants have begun adjusting the tip prompts on the digital payment processor sometimes leading to better earnings. If 18% must be added to every bill it should be done so as a mandatory gratuity at a lower rate. The best solution would be to implement a no tip policy and simply increase the menu prices by 18%.

OR
Write a letter or an email to city council that clearly explains why you AGREE or DISAGREE with the proposal to hold a Saturday farmers' market in the community centre parking lot.
response_text:
When tips are mandatory, they move away from their initial purpose of voluntary appreciation and more into the realm of pseudo-taxes. Thus, with workers wages stagnating, it makes sense, from the standpoint of an executive, to offload responsibility to the customer through mandatory tips rather than increasing pay. However, for both the customer and the worker, the experience becomes worse, and more expensive.

 

Without appreciation tied to actual human agency, work quality falls to baselines. Employees have no reason to go past the baseline if, what's supposed to be, a marker for work ethic and capability, is just the mandatory baseline. Thus, when workers don't get any real appreciation from the people they're working for, quality from the top employees sink. Additionally, quality sinks as a result of not only lack of motivation in the top-tier workers, but also because bottom-tier workers don't have real any reason to elevate their abilities past the baseline, resulting in mediocrity across the board. Not to mention the awkward customer-to-worker relationship, countless times a worker is going to have to explain to a new customer that indeed, you have no other choice but to tip, it's demoralizing for both parties involved. The customer feels as if their morals are being forcefully put to the test, stuck between supporting a fellow person with a tip but feeling greedily forced to do so. The worker feels as if they're scalping their customers but feeling, rightfully, entitled to a tip.

 

Not only does worker quality sink, but earnings sink as well. To successfully survive as a restaurant that has mandatory tipping, the policy would need mass mobilization across multiple franchises and chains, or else the business gets flushed out by restaurants who don't make you tip. Regardless of if there's even customers remaining past the tipping change, the amount would be so thin that it's unlikely for the business to break-even, let alone profit. Those same customers would also be spending far less to make up for the hefty 18% pseudo-tax, an amount that succeeds the GST in Canada, an actual tax. Then, business owners have to meddle with the messy reality of small orders; what if a customer wants a water or drink? What if they just want some fries? The brand would take a toll and consistent policy application would be different from store-to-store, creating a chaotic work environment.

 

Finally, without voluntary tips, you get the inevitable reality of customer expectations rising. In an ideal world, the business doesn't get out-competed, and there remains a consumer base after the tipping change, but that doesn't come free of charge, customers expect premium quality now because they're being forced to pay extra, and when in conjunction with the points above, it becomes fatal. The workers who now feel unappreciated are being hammered down to the heightened standards of the new customers, furthering the belief that they are not good enough. The workers who feel like they don't have to exceed expectations now are met with the harsh reality of customers' expectations, forcing them into either quitting, or growing a chip on their shoulder, further harming the business. 

 

In conclusion, when you force someone to tip, the experience, and the quality, of everyone involved, lowers. Workers grow unappreciated or lazy, customers grow picky or stingy, and overall, the business is severely harmed, on multiple levels. The discussion should not be about forcing customers, who are also workers elsewhere, to tip, but should be about forcing corporations to heighten wages for their workers, increasing the amount of money people can tip in the long-term.

Tips are designed as a way to thank a specific server at a restaurant for their service to a specific customer. This encourages your servers to work hard to make your customers enjoy the whole experience at your restaurant and to feel that they get rewarded for their efforts. However, if tips are mandated, it will discourage the extra effort servers put forward in order to get tips. Employee

The Necessity of the Mandatory Lunch Hour

        

    During lunch, have you ever been anxiously watching the clock as the last 5 minutes drain from your half hour break? I've been there. Not only does it seem like not enough time to eat or relax, it actually isn't. Depending on the length of your shifts, the speed of your eating, or your ability to wind down, this half hour is never enough. When considering safety, age, and general health, a 1-hour lunch break would benefit the safety and health of all.

 

  

     My colleagues and I often come back to our work environment with coffees and full stomachs. I'm sure you've been told "Don't swim for 1-hour after eating," well human bodies do take time to digest. 

    Science says digestion typically takes at least half an hour, but some foods need much more time. During these times it is recommended to avoid intense labour or stressful environments as it can disrupt digestion. Our digestive systems are full of enzymes and hormones that not only contribute to our physical state, but mental as well. So don't just avoid eating before swimming, avoid eating before all intensive labours!

 

 

Those who work 12-hour shifts (such as myself) often find that a half hour lunch break hardly feels like a break at all. Due to our lack of rest, many of us find ourselves far too exhausted during the last 1–2 hours of our shifts to do any significant work. We can trust these signals our bodies are sending because they are for good reason! 

    Many safety incidents occur during the last few hours of a shift. Whether you are rushing to get the last bits done, or to clean up for next shift, your lack of decent rest has been found to actually be more detrimental to yourself, your work, and potentially your colleagues. What is scariest of all, are the industries where these circumstances are most often found; medicine, nursing, mining, many trade jobs, etc. These folks are working tough hours, in physically and mentally intense industries, with breaks that simply fit the word of law, instead of their needs.

 

    

    Some may argue that longer breaks will slow down production, and this may be the case. However, many cases have found longer breaks to actually increase production, seemingly due to the fact that many workers come back rested and well-fed. It would be wise to educate some individuals who are acting against their own human needs, as these behaviours are often built by a "production-over-all," mindset which historically contributes to tragic endings. 

 

 

    If you care about the safety and well-being of your employees, colleagues, or even friends and family by proxy, consider extending the lunch break. It is a simple change, that may require a sacrifice to production, but will make everyone's lives healthier and safer in the long run.

The mandatory nature of this policy is disrespectful to the fiscal autonomy of employees because it disregards their right to spend their money how they would like to, it is unfair to employees because it requires all to participate, even those that do not feel affected by the supposed morale boost, and ultimately, it is an arbitrary policy that puts the responsibility of workplace satisfaction in the hands of hardworking, wage-earning employees instead of the business owner.

 

First, employees should be allowed to manage their income how they see fit. Many employees are not happy with this policy for that reason. One employee stated in an online chat that, "They can barely afford to buy gifts for their own family", and another remarked, "Let me choose how to spend my own money.". While putting money toward a collective fund may benefit all employees, and may even increase employee retention according to some surveys, it is still immoral because it does not take into account the needs of the individual employee. Certain employees are in greater need than others, and that fact may not be appropriately addressed by something like a social fund. Social funds provide things like parties, gifts, flowers and coffee stations, but they do not provide necessities. Sincerely,

Employee

My name is Fabriel Mackula, and I live at 43 Parkman Drive. I am, just as yourselves, a concerned citizen who desires nothing more but the best for our city.

 

I am addressing you today in light of recent news regarding the development plans for a golf course that would replace one of our few remaining public parks.

 

I would like to begin this letter by thanking you for taking into consideration all feedback from members of your community, without whom its growth and prosperity would not be what it is today.

 

I strongly disagree with the decision to replace the public park with an 18-hole golf course.

 

This public park is one of the last few remaining public parks in our city, most of which have already suffered by the hand of a rapid growth in housing and business development, which prioritizes profits over environmental concerns and free, openly accessible leisure for our community.

 

Statistics from polls in regard to this proposal suggests that our older generations are in favour of the golf course by a majority, however, there is a very clear and obvious backlash from our younger generations. A golf course will only benefit the few in our community who can both enjoy it, and afford it, strictly limiting its access to tourists and higher-income citizens. One of the first issues, would be the impact that this would have on local businesses. Mom and Pops Café, the Grocery store, the bank and several other essential businesses reside in the heart of where this proposed bike lane would go. Four to six months of construction would negatively affect these businesses first hand. The noises and general distraction of work, could cause a lack of customers and personal enjoyment for staff. I believe that mandatory tipping is an improvement overall to the way restaurants across Canada determine pay regarding their front-of-house workers. Servers are extremely important to the business, but their wages being left up to customer discretion does not reflect this. 

 

If someone is desperate to make ends meet (a very real scenario in this economy), they will push themselves beyond their typical boundaries in order to find and maintain a job. This is already an issue as not all employers have the best interest of their employees in mind, but when combining it with the fact that each potential customer has their own notions on the proper way for workers to conduct themselves, employees are left in a hard position.

 

Servers are tasked with providing "exceptional service" that may look one way for management, but is completely subjective when left up to those they serve. They could be pushing themselves to their limit each and every night, but if a customer doesn't like the way they smile, or if the server did not hear when they said "excuse me" one time, they may be penalized. With the introduction of mandatory tips, servers can do their work without the nagging thought that whatever they do may be scrutinized and deprive them of their earned income.

 

On the topic of customers (and as a customer myself), mandatory tips eliminate confusion and pressure around tipping, too. People going out for a bite to eat don't always want to do maths and judge another person based on their standards just to decide how much extra money they should be spending that night. People who are feeling less generous, or have had to tip 15% on everything they'd bought previously in the day, may also punish their servers for things beyond the workers' control. Tipping is also not mandatory in many countries, and expecting everyone to understand our relatively niche tipping culture just so that hard workers may be paid is also not realistic. 

 

Restaurants having mandatory tipping also ensures that employers are held accountable for paying their staff, which boosts trust in a workplace environment and keeps employees satisfied enough to continue working.

 

Thankfully, management at Cozy Corner Bistro has always been good to me, which is why I feel comfortable writing in with my thoughts. I believe that those who are nervous or upset about the new change are simply used to one way of doing things, and the system might've worked favourably for them. However, they don't understand that what helps those around them will help them, too. Reliability with earning and spending is a proper step forward for us, and I am very pleased with the policy change.

 

Regards, 

    Employee

Jude

        I am writing today to express my opposition to city's proposal to permanently close the city's largest public park for the development of an 18-hole golf course. Proponents argue that the economic advantages outweigh the social and environmental impacts, however, I believe the social and environmental impacts would have a negative effect on our community and environment that will ultimately create different economic problems in the future. I am asking city council to look beyond the short term economic gains the golf course could produce and consider our long-term community well-being. A public park that all community members have the opportunity to enjoy is a greater social good than a private golf course that caters to only select segments of our society. In an era of increasing wealth disparity and environmental degradation, we need to preserve the public community assets and local ecosystems to the best of our ability, and maintaining the park as a public space is the best way to ensure that we do. 

    Golf is an elitist sport; participation requires wealth and leisure time. Only people who have the finances and time will be able to use the proposed golf course. As reflected in the survey conducted, less than half of the population under the age of 54 agree with the proposal. People who are retired or have spent more time in the work force might find the golf course an attractive idea as they are the demographic who can enjoy it. Students, young families, and people in poverty do not have the same privileges. Taking away a public space that is accessible to everyone in place of a private institution that will only benefit a segment of our society will not make our community better. Families will no longer be able to use the space for free recreation and events such as children's birthday parties. People will no longer be able to exercise or walk their dogs in the area. Community events will be pushed indoors and may no longer be free if they are forced to find private venues to host. Proponents argue that the jobs and tourism created outweigh these social impacts, however, if these economic impacts are only benefiting certain segments of society, the social impact on those left behind will be stark. 

        The environmental impact of replacing the park with a golf course will be disastrous. We already know that bee and insect populations are decreasing in Canada and this will have a devastating impact on the future of agriculture in this country. Instead of turning the park into a golf course, city council should be investigating ways to preserve and develop natural ecosystems. Native plants are incredibly important to the environment. Creating butterfly and bee gardens that everyone can enjoy is better for our ecological and social future. Golf courses have limited garden space and focus on grass upkeep instead. Grass maintenance requires a lot of water and is not environmentally friendly. Also, grass does little for local ecosystems. Plants and trees have a positive effect on local ecosystems. We need to preserve the outdoor spaces that we have in order to secure our environmental future and avoid spending public money on future environmental problems that could have been avoided if we thought ahead today.

        A public space that includes everyone is ultimately better than a private space that excludes certain members of society. Some people may like the golf course more than the park, and some people may benefit from jobs or increased tourism, but if only some are benefiting that means people are being left behind. We have already learned how being careless about the environment has long-term negative impacts. Often, the results of environmental negligence are extremely costly to fix or irreversible. We cannot let the short term economic gains for some to outweigh the long term social and environmental consequences that will affect society as a whole. Instead of investing in a golf course, I implore you to invest in our community and public spaces in order to create a better society for everyone.

    Under the current parameters for this fund, the money in it could go to parties, gifts, flowers, and communal hardware such as a coffee machine. This opens the fund up to easy embezzlement, as anyone could just claim something is a gift and use money from the fund for it, even if they just keep it for themselves. There are also two benefits which come to mind, the first being efficiency and the second being pride.

 

I will begin with the three concerns, starting with comfort.


In the Staff Meeting Minutes it has been stated that "Shirts may be tucked in or worn out depending on the employee preference and comfort"
Giving employees this option is great as for some individuals they may find themselves feeling uncomfortable at how revealing a tucked in shirt can be. They may find that their body shape is more visibile while the shirt is tucked in. It is potentially a source of insecurity for them. 

By giving employees this choice, the concern of insecurity over body type visibility is mitigated. 
 

The next concern is finances - Additional clothing must be purchased by employee's. Some companies require a person to place a deposit on their initial uniform which is reimbursed when they leave the company. 
This is a source of stress for some as we are in a recession and every dollar a person can save up is meaningful. When people lack the income for even hobbies an initial $50.00 expenditure could result in them avoiding a purchase that is beneficial to their hobbies & interests in the pay period where they would be required to purchase the uniform. 
The decision provide the initial uniform free of charge mitigates this concern in my opinion. The employee is only to make an expenditure when replacing or changing their work outfit which is very fair. 
 

The final concern is related to creativity.
It is stated in the Workplace Journal that "While uniform dress codes can create team spirit and instill a sense of pride, they may also stifle individuality and reduce creativity. Dress codes can create a more comfortable and professional work environment, but a perceived lack of choice may create resentment and reduce productivity."

My opinion on the stifled individuality and reduced creativity is that it is irrelevant to the workplace. When we belong to a company, we are under their jurisdiction. This means that we have certain expectations that we follow as their employees. There are certain feelings that we are meant to leave behind when we step foot into a workplace. Creativity, while nice, is something that is best left for our own creative endeavours. If an individual feels that they must express creativity through dress wear at the work place then perhaps they are misplacing their creative forces. They can take that feeling of individuality and instead put it towards their interactions and what they produce as a worker. 
Ultimately the most meaningful expression of creativity is in what that person outputs, not what they wear.

This option to choose a skirt or pants as well as a long-sleeved or short-sleeved shirt is a plus for creativity. One could mix and match clothing combinations to match their own at-home dressing. 
For example, a skirt and a long sleeved shirt could be more comfortable for a person. A pair of pants and a long sleeved shirt would be my own choice personally. I find that combination to be quite similar to my regular attire.

I will now discuss potential benefits of a dress code policy. 

The first point I will make is related to efficiency.
In a kitchen there is often a unique uniform provided to the head chef(s) as opposed to the more general roles such as utility & line cook. This is useful in identifying who is whom - Often in a high paced environment we don't always have the time to visually distinguish who is who based upon features alone. 
Knowing who the head chef is based upon the uniform is useful as you can more quickly get your tasks done. 
However we work in an office space. There is a specific benefit to having a uniform in our workplace. This benefit has to do with identifying new employees & distinguishing between clientele and employee. 
Under the current policy it is hard to tell apart a clientele from an employee. 
Giving a specific uniform mitigates this. Additionally if someone is a new higher they may find themselves needing assistance with getting around the office. They may not know who to approach - the unique 
 

The second benefit is pride. 
From my experiences in the workplace having a branded uniform is generally seen as a good thing. In the Connecting Careers User Poll it states that for the age group 25-39 62% of those polled were in support of workplace dress codes & or uniforms. 
I personally have only worked with people in my age group, 25-39. 
Back then myself and coworkers had commentated between one another that we look great in our uniforms. Sometimes we would find ourselves still in our uniforms while running errands after work & this led to running into one another. It's much easier to notice a coworker when they are wearing the logo & colour's of the company. 

It's a conversation starter as well with strangers - they see that one is employed and become curious sometimes as to the nature of the work they do. 
Perhaps they are curious about the company and interested to apply as well. 
It creates visibility in public spaces of the company & is also free advertising.

To Whom It May Concern,

 

Hello, I am a citizen of the city in which your council represents, and I am writing to voice my support for the proposed farmers market on Saturdays

 

It has been shown in other municipalities around the world that a community ran farmers market can have lasting positive effects on the population of the city, both financially, culturally, and socially. A strong community ran marketplace can help empower small business and hobby farmers, while providing a local option for shoppers in an era of large corporate monopolies. These local options can help bring down the prices of large scale grocery stores by giving them much needed competition. 

 

The planned use of the publicly owned community centre is also a great idea in my opinion, as it deepens the connection between the vendors and the public, who's taxes go to upkeep and maintenance. This creates accountability for vendors to serve the public and produce quality goods at fair prices, and allows for regular use of these facilities by everyone in the general public, not just those who rent the facility or are part of a club/organization that uses it as a meeting place. 

 

While I definitely agree it will be tougher to find parking for the senior citizens meeting at the centre on the same days, it is important to note the appeal of the farmers market is for all citizens, and while unfortunate for this group, I feel it is a necessary compromise for the benefit of the entire population. The argument for the parking lot being "inaccessible for tax payers on Saturdays" is invalid in my opinion, because if you needed to use that parking lot, you would already have to be attending an event at the community centre in the first place (such as a seniors meeting as previously mentioned). And if the community centre is booked for an event such as this, it would be unavailable anyway.

 

There are also concerns I've read in comments about prices at the farmers market, which is a completely separate issue from the topic at hand. While I will try to stay on track here, it is important to note that these price differences stem from the costs incurred by small scale farming and craft making. Large corporations like Walmart and Loblaws manufacture goods at unfathomably large scales, impossible for individuals or small teams to compete with. Factory farming and textile machines drive costs down for sure, but they lead to inferior quality and are unimaginably expensive, especially to a vendor in a small town like ours. A lettuce farmer with a small field will never be able to compete price wise with a company that owns hundreds of large scale greenhouses, but they can compete in terms of quality and consumer trust. 

 

The $40 fee for vendors will also be incredibly beneficial for both the community centre and the municipal funding as well. The financial burden of parking lot upkeep will be transferred to the vendors, freeing up tax money for other city spending. This should be great news to those who voiced concerns about tax money going to the project, as these funds can be reallocated to things like roads, trash collection, and other city projects (instead of being spent on a parking lot that is only used by those able to rent the centre, or those who are part of a club as previously stated). This will also create a responsibility on vendors to care for the property, as they are now the ones funding it.

 

 I feel the price is also set fairly, as $40 is a reasonable amount to ask from a small business. Any higher, and it would risk alienating those unsure about their ability to recoup the costs, while any lower would allow low quality merchandise to flood the market by those with less to lose. The 100 vendor spaces will also allow for large variety and diversity in product offerings, leading to healthy competition between vendors. While I have my issues with the free market system, I do believe strong competition between businesses/vendors will lead to increased quality and lower prices with time. This large vendor space will also lead to an equally large funding for the community centre. 

 

My final argument will be that of promoting healthier food options, and of personal choice. The market will not replace the more affordable (albeit less nutritious) options provided by large corporate grocery stores, but will serve as an alternative for those with the means to afford healthier food. It will also serve as a way for those in the community to pressure these larger businesses to provide healthier options, as to not lose out on market share and customers.

 

In conclusion, I believe this is an excellent idea for the community and for small local business alike, and I urge you to consider these points in your final decision.

I am writing to address the current proposal of implementing a dress code and uniforms at our company. I, as a long time employee, understand and support the proposal for several reasons. Without uniforms there are many possible disruptions to the workplace, and creating a standard dress code with a uniform can have significant benefits as well as prevent disruptions. First, people may find it difficult to prepare an appropriate work wardrobe and this can distract others or cause conflicts. Second, having a dress code and uniforms can help solve many issues with the logistics involving your work wardrobe. Finally, dress codes will help to foster a team environment at work while still allowing some self-expression.

 

We have all had or heard of problems arising from inappropriate work attire. There have been stories on the news where individuals have had such outlandish outfits and then claimed they are entitled to express themselves however they want as a protected class. A dress code and uniform solves this issue. Additionally, gossip and harassment are significant concerns in the workplace. Men wearing a shirt that is too tight and women wearing low cut skirts are just a few examples of inappropriate attire that can cause disruptions. Also, there are people who may be great at their job but may not care or have the ability to create a wardrobe for work is acceptable to everyone. Having a dress code with uniforms addresses all and solves most of these issues.

Picking out what to wear for work, going shopping for your work clothes, making sure clothes are laundered and fashionable are a few of the logistical issues a dress code and uniform addresses. While some people may enjoy being flashy or staying up to date on the latest trends, many people would rather not have to worry about this at all. Some people's financial situation could be a significant barrier to having a socially acceptable work wardrobe. Having a dress code and uniform would free you from these logistical issues involving your work attire.

 

Lastly, feeling workplace camaraderie and having a strong sense of being part of a team helps everyone work together, while fostering a positive environment in the workplace. Coming into work and seeing everyone with our company logo on their shirt is a subtle but strong symbol that visually shows we are all here to work for a common goal, our company's success. Self-expression is also preserved with the ability to wear jewellery, different hairstyles, and you can even decide to wear your shirt tucked in or untucked.

 

Our company will greatly benefit from this proposal to implement a dress code and uniforms. Our workers will be in an environment with less hassle and stress without the worry of what to wear, or if they will be accepted or made fun of about their choices. Implementing a dress code and uniform removes so many obstacles to a peaceful and productive workplace. No longer will we have to devote time outside work in order to purchase an appropriate wardrobe or stay up to date on the latest fashions. Finally, we shouldn't forget the powerful camaraderie that can come with a dress code and uniforms.  As you can tell, I am firmly behind the proposal to implement a dress code and uniforms at our company and I am eagerly looking forward to this being implemented.

Thank you for your request for and consideration of our feedback,

Will Baryo

    This brings me to the environmental impact the golf course would have on our city. To convert that same park into a golf course would mean the destruction of many of the trees and wildlife habitats in the area which would displace many of our native species. Both the increase in water usage and destruction of important habitats would be harmful to our environment and would be viewed negatively by many citizens and environmental groups. 

   

    In conclusion, I believe the cons outweigh the pros in regard to this proposal. The park is a beautiful piece of nature we can not afford to lose, and it is clear that the vast majority of our citizens agree it should stay. Write a letter or an email to city council that clearly explains why you AGREE or DISAGREE with the proposal to hold a Saturday farmers' market in the community centre parking lot.
response_text:
Cozy Corner Bistro Management:

Personally, I disagree with the proposal of having a mandatory 18% tip rate. Let me explain a little further.

 

I believe that not having a mandatory minimum tip rate is more beneficial for a plethora of reasons. Some families that come out to eat could be less financially secure than some of our other patrons. Having a mandatory tip rate will price lower income earners out of our market. Single people and couples are a little different, but this especially applies to people with large families. Often times these families can still afford to leave a small tip, and when times aren't as tough, they often tip really well. Having a mandatory 18% tip will surely price some larger families out of being able to afford our food.

 

Another valid reason not to implement the mandatory 18% is also for my coworkers. Most of our staff at the restaurant currently are excellent. They work hard for what they earn, and they're proud when someone goes above and beyond with the tip they leave. If we were to flip that on it's head and implement a mandatory 18%, people would become complacent. Humans seek habit and comfort. Some are great, and some not so much. I think there's a very real possibility that some of our staff will work less hard knowing they're guaranteed at least 18% on top of their base pay. That will reflect badly on the restaurant. The staff that are going above and beyond deserve the tip that’s above and beyond. The ones that don't go above and beyond, deserve what they get. "Good enough" shouldn't be good enough.

 

We also have to see this from the customers point of view. If the service at a restaurant truly is next to non-existent, my tip will reflect that. I would be speaking with the manager if my server were in the bathroom the entire time I was at my table. Making me flag down other restaurant employees so I can get a drink refill. Just for my waiter to come out of the bathroom or finish his cigarette outside and slap the debit machine in front of me wielding a minimum 18% tip rate. "Haha, no thanks", would be my response. If we were having this discussion about Gordan Ramsay's Hells Kitchen in Las Vegas, or Nobu in Malibu, I think we could have a serious conversation about a mandatory tip rate. I, personally, just don't think this is the kind of establishment to implement something like that.

 

Some of the stats show that even unprompted, most people tip in the 10-15% range. Also, with the rising price of necessities like groceries and gas these days. Lots of people are experiencing "tip fatigue", myself included. I'm even more likely to leave a tip within the 15-20% range unprompted. If you were to shove a machine in my face with a base 18%, that's what you're going to get. While having a base tip would likely bring up our bi-weekly pay. It sounds like this is a band-aid fix that our establishment is placing into the customers lap while avoiding the real problem of them not wanting to pay us a livable base wage. Which is unfair for everyone involved. Between potentially pricing families out, making a broken system even more broken, and taking away the choice from the customer. I think this is a gesture better left undone. Maybe one day North America would approach tipping how Europe does, but I digress.

 

All the best with whatever decision you guys go with! I'm here every step of the way. With regards,

 

Andrew
