To whom it may concern,

 

    City Council has recently put forward a proposal to host a weekly Saturday farmer's market in the Community Centre's parking lot from May until October. 

 

    I support hosting the farmer's market in the Community Centre's parking lot on Saturdays. Having a local farmer's market will grant our town easy, convenient access to locally grown produce, it will help foster community, reduce our carbon footprint, and also bring in a substantial amount of extra money to our town.

 

    Foremost, convenient access to fresh, locally grown produce is essential in keeping our men, women and children happy and healthy. Some people have concerns about the cost of produce at farmer's markets being higher than the prices at the supermarkets, however, we have to take something into consideration; every dollar spent at a farmer's market goes directly into the pockets of our neighbours. When we purchase produce from a local farmer's market, we are essentially cutting out the middle man, and keeping our hard-earned dollars directly within our community. We are directly helping our neighbours put food on their tables, and clothes on their children's backs, rather than supporting the economy of, for example, Mexico, or the United States of America.

 

    Furthermore, a farmer's market in our town will foster community. Residents of our town will have direct access and the ability to connect with farmers and vendor owners at the market. Making informed choices about the food we feed our families is so important when we think about eating nutritiously and health consciously. What better way to make informed choices, than being able to directly ask the farmer who grew the produce, or the person who made the item? Fostering a community where we can share, ask, help others and make connections is absolutely pivotal to our growing town. 

 

    Additionally, having a farmer's market in our town's core will greatly reduce our carbon footprint that is tied to food transportation. Every day, millions of transport trucks, boats and airplanes deliver food from fields to supermarkets all around the world. Often times, food is being imported from countries across the world. Although there are some type of things, such as tropical fruits, that we cannot grow, there is an abundant amount of delicious vegetables and fruits that we can and do grow locally. When we buy at our local farmer's markets, not only are we keeping our money in our community, we are eliminating the need to emit so many harmful emissions into the air we breathe, thus maintaining a cleaner and healthier Earth.

 

    Finally, hosting this farmer's market from May to October every Saturday will bring in a substantial amount of extra money for our town, which will boost our economy. Since City Council will be charging each vendor $40 per week, and they will have 100 vendor spots, the income from the farmer's market will be approximately $4,000 per week, if the vendor spots are filled. $16,000 a month, which is $96,000 per year, is a great amount of extra money that can be used for parking lot maintenance, as well as establishing systems to alleviate some of the concerns of residents. For example, senior residents have mentioned that they would not be happy to lose parking spots at the Community Centre on Saturday's. Some of the income from the vendor table fees could be used to create some dedicated senior's parking spaces to ensure that they have ample parking for their Saturday activities.  

 

    In conclusion, I proudly support the farmer's market coming to the Community Centre. Our town will benefit greatly from having convenient access to fresh, locally grown produce. The farmer's market will help foster the community that people crave, it will help us reduce our carbon footprint, as well as create another stream of income the town can use to maintain the area, and address citizen concerns. 

    

Sincerely,

Tiara Johnston

Many of the cities residents may be unable to equitably access goods and services under protected grounds of disability, and equally, lose access/ease of accessing social services which they are entitled to as a member of the public, if the only option to access these good and services is by biking or walking; In line with the AODA, we must ensure the downtown core remains accessible. Access to emergency vehicles may also be restrictive, impacting response times to police, fire, and ems. Since its inception, Main St has relied on vehicle traffic in order to generate commerce and allow citizens access to social services. Careful consideration of the consequences of this conversion must be conducted. 

 

Furthermore, proponents of this measure have failed to consider alternative, middle ground approaches. Urban centres such as the city of Toronto, Oshawa, Kingston, and Ottawa, have introduced car free areas to their downtown cores, at the taxpayers expense, only to have to modify the conditions of the restriction through both infrastructure and policy. This is a severely inefficient use of public funds which these cities were entrusted to protect and manage responsibly. A mixed-use roadway that maintains vehicle traffic while introducing bike infrastructure, such as curb separated lanes, traffic signals, and right of ways, may be far more appropriate. This reasonable and prudent approach would likely satisfy a majority of proponents for conversion as well as appeal to detractors of the proposals totalitarian approach to urban planning. I believe the proposal to completely close Main St to vehicles is grounded in ideals and absolutes rather than a full consideration of the circumstances. 

 

As a final point, many in support of this conversion have concerns, which are shared by myself, relating to the environment and the conservation of natural spaces by decreasing pollution. However, I do not believe it to be logical that rerouting traffic will cause a significant impact in this area. Canada, as a country, produces among the lowest amount of emissions of any nation. The environmental impact of this proposal will likely be negligible to larger, global factors, especially as the same traffic will continue to utilize surrounding roadways. I propose that the proposed budget of this conversion project be redirected to more meaningful and impactful initiatives. With parks and wetland conservation areas within the city, we can ensure they receive appropriate protection from future commercial development by redirecting finite resources away from proposals which fail to stand on grounds of environmental protection. 

 

Upon examination of the economic impact on local businesses, the potentially restrictive and unlawful barriers to those with disabilities, the availability of reasonable alternative solutions, and the negligible environmental impact, I am firmly against the proposal to make Main St a bike-only area. If the council believes the case of the proposal is stronger than its detractions, I believe it to be reasonable that a pilot program be conducted for a period of 6–18 months, before investing considerable financial resources on infrastructure.  It is important that cyclists and pedestrians have safe and unimpeded access to Main St, but it is also important to recognize how vehicle traffic has shaped the cityscape as it stands today.  Thank you for your time. 

 

Aaryn Sokolowski

Dear management,

 

    I am writing against your proposed policy to implement mandatory 18% tips to all restaurant bills. I have taken the time to carefully review your suggestion, and there a few points I would like to bring forward to allow you to understand my position. I believe that implementing mandatory tips will eliminate incentive for a stronger work ethic among employees; discourage the more experienced, stronger staff; and deter customers from visiting.

 

    Restaurants provide a unique source of income to its servers. While the base wages are the same, each server is tipped according to the customer's interpretation of their service. This provides a great incentive for employees to go the extra mile and provide exceptional service. Although every customer won't have the same opinion or standard regarding the assistance they're given, tipping does provide a fairly accurate representation of what each server deserves. Mandating a set tip on each bill decreases the incentive for providing friendly service to clients, as the server will be guaranteed a tip either way. 

 

    Second, setting a mandatory tip will discourage those who would usually receive a higher tip. Experienced employees learn different ways to provide the best service, through time and effort. Since every employee receives the same base wage, friendliness and a willingness to ensure their guests receive great service is the only way for servers to earn more. With the current tipping system, employees are generally guaranteed to make fair compensations for their service. Eliminating this may result in talented servers becoming discouraged, or in some cases, leaving their position. 

 

    Finally, implementing a set tip on each bill will likely deter customers from visiting the restaurant. Clients enjoy the freedom of being able to provide exceptional servers with a higher bonus while not feeling forced to tip as much to a server they feel did not satisfy their expectations and needs. Studies show that nearly every customer tips their server, but the amount tipped is what varies. Forcing the customer to tip their server 18%, regardless of their performance, may feel unfair and illogical. This may result in less business for your company. 

 

    In conclusion, I hope you will consider the risks that accompany the implementation of mandatory tipping. Decreased work incentive, discouraged seasoned employees, and deterring of customers would not be helpful in the promotion or growth of this restaurant. However, I do understand the attraction of this proposal, for some. Being guaranteed a fairly high tip would be encouraging and provide stability. I personally know the frustration of being tipped less than I believed my performance deserved. Yet, in light of my aforementioned concerns, I would instead suggest raising the base wages of employees. This way, even if the tips received by some servers are lower than others, they will still be receiving a higher salary. In addition, the incentive for the best service is still maintained by all, and customers still have the freedom to tip as they interpret their servers to be deserving. 

 

    Thank you for considering my concerns regarding this proposal. I would be happy to discuss this further at our next weekly review meeting.

 

Best regards,

Lianna W

Dear Manager.

I would like to take this time to respond to the recent Manager Memo that was sent out.

 I would like you to know not all staff are on board with this idea, including myself.  I strongly have to disagree with this request and I would like to explain some of the reasons why.

First, I can understand where you are coming from, and at first thought it may seem like a great way to boost moral and keep staff motivated and happy, but the truth is quite the opposite.  On paper, I'm sure it looks like a winning solution for those somewhat slower tip days, but let's break it down.

As long as I have been working at the Cozy Corner Bistro, I've noticed a steady flow of tips coming in, showing that more than half of our customers (58%) are tipping as high as 15%, 20%, and even 25%, regularly. And on the slower days, still 30% of customers leaving 5%, 10%, and 15%.

As you can see, most (88%) of our customers are tipping, Which in turn lets me know that they are happy with the meal and the service they have received.  This also means that there is a good chance they will tell more people about us,  creating more business from word of mouth,  and they will most likely be back  to eat again. 

 I think it's very important to let customers decide whether to tip or not and don't upset the herd, so to speak. 

 Also, With the current state of the economy, there are a lot of people struggling financially right now and adding a mandatory 18% tip to the bill could be business suicide for the Cozy Corner Bistro as I would argue that most customers would have a problem with it.  Most men take pride in leaving a tip they feel is reasonable.  In my opinion, taking that power away from them would have a negative impact on the business.

Let me share an experience I had with a different, but similar issue - A few years ago I worked at a very popular casino as a high stakes poker dealer.  Poker is one of the few table games in the casino that has a high tip payout, meaning that the dealer receives a tip almost ever single hand.  And some would be large, depending on the size of the pot.  But for the most part it was a dollar. So that’s a dollar for every hand you deal.  When I started at the casino, the tips you earned you got to keep.  And for reference, when I first started dealing poker, most of the other staff were very happy and relieved there was some new staff to deal poker as most of them despised dealing that game as it was only $1/hand tips.  

As you can probably predict, my constant flow of tips were becoming a problem for those dealers not receiving tips.  I was very professional but kept the game moving at a good pace and kept the players happy, chatting between hands etc. My regular player liked me - therefore my tips grew. So staff complained that it was unfair that I got to deal poker all the time.  Within no time at all, they implemented a new rule stating that tips were now to be pooled and divided with all live game dealers based on their hours.  

This ended up being a huge disaster, as the live game dealers now refused to go above and beyond and customer service hit an all-time low.  Staff moral dropped.

Second, once staff found out tips were being pooled, most of my regular tipping players refused to tip me knowing I had to share with a dealer they didn't like. 

Within 8 short months of this new tipping regulations, the live games table games were actually costing the casino money, as they had no players but still had to pay the dealers to stand at a dead table. 

One year after this was implemented, live games had completely dissolved and was replaced with digital games, resulting in job loss for the dealers, therefore effecting the restaurant sales and resulting in waitresses layoffs.  

The last time i stopped at this Casino in my travels I was shocked to see all staff and no patrons.   

So as I explained, I strongly disagree with this mandatory 18% tip based on my previous experience.  I would argue that tips are gratuity that are earned when staff go above and beyond and show outstanding customer service, and making that mandatory would rub a lot of people the wrong way and in my opinion, promote poor work ethic.  

I hope before this is implemented you reach out to chat with me further on this with any more questions or concerns.  I am hoping you reconsider based on my information.  

Thanks for your time.

Regards, 

Kelvin

Dear Management,

 

     I am writing in regard to the recent gratuity discussion that has taken place at our restaurant. I understand that as next week starts, all customers will be required to pay an 18% gratuity on top of their bill. Even though this new standard of operations will be in course for next week, I thought I should bring up some concerns me and some other staff have on the matter, and why we are against the mandatory gratuity option.

 

     Firstly, I'd like to note that the presence of tips should never be a factor of expected income. As a profitable business that is able to pay their employees a fair wage, the expected income should be what you have been promised to take home hourly. The aspect of tips is a bonus on top, in relation to how good your service was to the customer, and therefore the paying customer themselves should have full say in the amount they decide to tip. When we look at what the customer is paying for, their money goes towards the space, the food, and the payroll for staff. When we price our food at higher or lower price points, they are not just paying for the food, they're paying for an expected result on service and space quality as well. 

    

    The customers choice of gratuity has been pushed by social norms to be expected, even despite the quality of work that is provided. Proposing this lack of choice will perpetuate the customers thoughts of not getting what they pay for (tipping fatigue), especially when the tipping percentage we are asking for is 3% higher than the average tip percentage at restaurants. This, in my opinion, lessens the range of customers that would choose our restaurant, and for us to "communicate this change as needed" can lead to blind siding regular customers who have been part of the previous operations. All of this can and will affect the relationship customers have with our establishment. 

 

     The notion of providing "great service without worrying about how much we'll make" is a double edge sword, as setting the mandatory tip to 18% will make staff more complacent, while making customers expect better work. As a business you would want your staff to work for their bonuses, rather than force the customer to eat the cost while not feeling like they get something in return. I'm worried even for myself it would create lazy habits and remove my interest in working hard to try and get the best possible tip. I think that leaving the tip option up to the customers allows for a healthy competitive work space where people earn their bonuses instead of being handed their bonus due to policy. 

    

    While I also understand there is the risk factor of having customers come in, us working hard for their satisfaction, to ultimately not receive any tip. And I see how the mandatory tip is the next line of thought management has gone down, I do believe there are other ways of encouraging or mandating tips when intense work and effort from staff are required. Having groups larger than six being asked to pay an auto-gratuity, or occupying tables for excessive periods of time resulting in a fee which is then split between the staff and the business, these are both examples of other routes we can take to get the desired outcome without forcing the customer into a mandatory 18% gratuity. 

 

    In conclusion my statement is this. While I understand there are staff who wish to receive steady compensation from customers for their work, I feel as though mandating the tip option will have negative affects on; staff work ethic, customer experience/relation with business, and possibility of receiving more from the customer for significantly above average work. Please take into consideration my thoughts on this matter, and feel free to reach out with any questions or new propositions as well. 

 

Thank you for your time.

 Sincerely, Concerned Staff

Many people that I talk to are on very strict diets where the timing of eating matters and for many of them, 12-1 does not work as they need it to. A matter I find even more concerning is religion. A lot of my coworkers use their break time to pray. Attention: City council members,

My name is Micaiah, and I have recently learned of the proposal to replace the local park with an 18 hole golf course. This came as a shock, as I have always thought of this park as beloved by many members of the community and an essential park of our town. I have read the proposal by the town, and while I understand some aspects of what has been released, I believe that the city council is missing several keys aspects of what makes this park so special. I do not agree with this proposal, and would kindly ask for your consideration to my concerns made below.

 

Firstly, I would like to address the argument that a golf course would "create ...  long term employment opportunities". I believe this golf course would actually result in net-negative employment numbers for the town. The park currently employs many individuals for the maintenance of the outbuildings, cleaning of the washrooms and the grounds keeping. This does not mention any of the summertime employment opportunities that are given to our youth for the programs held in the park by the town or local businesses. Removing our park, removes these jobs from our community. 

 

I would also like to address the environmental aspects of the proposed golf course. With the park's location so central to our community, I fear what the chemicals used on the golf course could do to our air and water quality. This says nothing of the effects to the local wildlife population that currently calls the park home. Also, we must take into consideration that our community park is home to many mature and beautiful trees, that by necessity would be cut down to create enough room for an 18 hole course. This golf course, could contaminate our water supply, disperse hundreds of animals, and cut the tree count of the town in half. I have not seen from the city or the developer any documents or studies to the contrary of these points. I would think it prudent that a full scale environmental study have been completed before ever releasing this proposal to the community. Removing our park, removes our safe drinking water, much of the towns wildlife and many of our trees.

 

It may be argued that a golf course would bring a new tourism aspect to our town. I would counter this by suggesting our park, surrounded by dozens of local shops, is our main tourism draw. With our many coffee shops, restaurants, and hotels so close to the park and all hosting or supporting events directly in the park, what would the removal of this space do? Consider the many charity runs, the Canada Day parade, and our "Buster Days" weekend celebration. All of these events are tourism draws, all of them supported by local businesses bordering the park. Just two weekends ago I, and I'm sure many of you, were present at the "Buster Days" parade, that saw so many of our children enthralled, as we watched our local community come together and celebrate our towns birthday. Events like that would not be possible without our local park. Removing our park, removes our parades, robs our businesses of tourism and deprives our children of such fond memories that we all share.

 

Our town is a special place, home to an old school prairie culture. The park has been the heart and soul of that culture, hosting our children’s play time, our friends birthdays and many of our major community celebrations. With the economic impact to our jobs and businesses, the environmental toll to our wildlife and trees and the community deprived of a treasured gathering place, the cost of the golf course would be far too great for our town to handle. I believe my thoughts here are shared by many voices of the community, reflected in the disapproval rating being nearly 60% in the community poll.  Consequently, I ask the council members to reconsider and drop this proposal.

 

Thank you,

Micaiah Audette

For example, If you go to a restaurant for lunch and the wait staff are slow to take your order or disappears for most of your meal. At that point aren't you more likely to leave a smaller tip? Rather than when the staff are quick and efficient as well as tentative to the needs of you and your table.

Staff A

Customer Retention

Lower Quality of Service

    By setting in place a mandatory 18% tipping policy, management runs the risk of lowering the quality of service rendered to customers. Conclusion

To whom it may concern,

I am writing as a concerned citizen to express my disapproval of the plan to make Main Street a bike only lane. Firstly, the location of the proposed change is poorly chosen, and will cause both inconvenience to drivers and a safety hazard for cyclists. On the corner of Main and Lilac is a grocery store and fire department, high traffic areas for civilian and emergency vehicles. The proposed change considers only that cyclists will be within the proposed location without accounting for the fact that they will still have to cross this high traffic intersection, leading to more exposure to traffic accidents, congestion for drivers, and of particular concern from my experience as an ambulance dispatcher, a potential slowdown or entire rerouting of emergency vehicles, who can no longer take the most direct route.  

 

Some business owners have expressed concerns over their livelihoods, depending on vehicle traffic for a significant portion of their income. The main culprit of this is the issue of parking; while many businesses still have side road access for the many people who did not or could not plan their whole day around taking a bike to work or school, they would have to park on a small side road to access any business in the bike only zone and walk. This would, again, cause congestion issues, or simply a loss of income for businesses on this stretch of road.

 

Finally, if we are going to be increasing taxes and diverting funds from other important projects; investing in more reliable, convenient public transport would be a better option. Not only would it reduce air-pollution - as is the goal of this initiative, but it would also positively impact the city in areas where the bike lane becomes a detriment. More frequent use of public transport would reduce the amount of cars on the road, thereby reducing traffic. It would not require a purchase in the hundreds of dollars for citizens who want to make use of the initiative their taxes help pay for like it would in the case of needing to purchase a bike, nor would those wishing to access Main Street need to plan their whole day around accessing that one street or pray that parking is semi-reasonable. We can simply have bus access. This would also mitigate the financial damage to businesses that rely on street traffic by allowing a similar flow of business.

 

In conclusion, the proposed initiative simply does not work for the layout of Main Street, increasing the likelihood of collisions between cars and cyclists in high traffic areas, slowing down the flow of traffic, and potentially disrupting emergency services from the fire department. It would harm local business and congest the area with parked cars in a location that simply doesn't have the layout to support it, and there are already other, less disruptive, more beneficial options to achieve the same result in a way that will not turn downtown and the surrounding area into a nightmare for anybody unwilling or unable to shell out hundreds of dollars for a bike, or those whose schedules do not allow them to travel this way.

 

Thank you for your attention,

 

Brandon.

Mandatory tips are detrimental to our business because they remove the very reason tips were created. The definition of a tip according to the Collins Dictionary is "a payment given for services in excess of the standard charge; gratuity." Essentially, the nature of a tip is to be an extra payment on top of the standard charge used to express gratitude. However, a mandatory tip is not an extra payment since it is required. Consequently, if implemented, our company would merely be increasing the standard price, but under a different name. Ultimately, mandatory tips should be avoided because they eliminate the intrinsic nature of a tip.

 

Additionally, due to this absence of freedom, customers will leave our business decreasing our overall profit. Some individuals may not want to leave extra payment as one staff member noted. The report on modern workplace trends records that "some employees are experiencing 'tip fatigue,' which can affect overall gratuity levels." Even without mandatory tips, customers are annoyed with the social pressure they receive to tip. Accordingly, when tips are required many individuals will be completely tired of the system and permanently leave our business. Overall, mandatory tips decrease our customers and in turn decrease our profit.

 

With the comfort of a guaranteed profit increase, some employees will find less reason to expend their best efforts. They no longer have the encouragement of better tips if they work harder. For example, poor customer service might increase because a staff member interacts more nonchalantly with a customer instead of friendly approaching them. In turn, customers will be dissatisfied with our services, so be more likely to permanently leave. Sincerely,

 

Micah Langdon

Employee

Dear City Council

 

    My name is Randy Siemens, and I am a member of the local community. I am writing this letter to express my upport for the proposal raised at last week's city council meeting. Specifically, I am writing about Proposal 4.0, regarding a farmers' market at the community centre.

 

    I am in full support of this proposal for many reasons. Most importantly, having the ability to sell fresh produce and artisanal goods right in town every week is a huge opportunity for local producers and artisans. What better way to support the future of our community than by supporting local businesses, and boosting the local economy!

 

    The farmers' market's website states that "farmer's markets are becoming a staple in many towns." I would argue, rather, that they already are a staple within many towns. I can't personally remember the last town I lived in that didn't have a local farmers' market on the weekend.

 

    From personal experience, the connections and benefits that you gain from attending a farmers' market regularly go far beyond that of just a normal consumer-vendor relationship. Instead of dealing with faceless corporations, you can actually speak directly to the people responsible for growing the food you put on your family's table! Some of the people I have met through farmers' markets in the past have become my closest friends. Bringing the community closer together benefits everyone.

 

    Some community members have voiced concerns that farmers' markets are more expensive than grocery stores, and that some in the community may struggle to afford to shop there. As someone who has been in a similar predicament, this is an unfortunate situation to find yourself in. However, I don't believe that the opportunity should be wasted for others who are able to afford to shop locally.

 

    One opinion that I found in my research within the community, comes from u$ername91 on the town's online chat. There, the user asked "Our tax dollars pay for the community centre. Why should we lose access to the parking lot on Saturdays?" I assume that the user in question did not read fully through the proposal highlights, as their question is answered within. Highlight 3 of the proposal states that each vendor will be charged a weekly $40 table fee to go towards the maintenance of the parking lot. Therefore, it would not actually be our tax dollars that are paying for the parking lot between the hours of 7:00 AM and 7:00 PM on Saturdays from May through October. Additionally, with space for up to 100 vendors, that is a weekly revenue potential of $4000, for approximately 24 weeks. This equates to $96,000 of yearly revenue potential from a parking lot that would otherwise cost money. This could then in turn be used to help expand the community centre's offerings. Alternatively, it could help alleviate the strain from the community centre on our tax dollars.

 

    My one and only concern with the proposal is regarding the senior citizens within the community. They regularly use the community centre as a gathering hub, and not having access to the parking lot on Saturdays could disrupt some of their routines. While they would still have access to the community centre, they will have to utilize street parking, which is not necessarily convenient for them. 

 

    With that being said, the farmers' market is only one day of the week, and there are possible solutions that I think should be explored with some senior advocacy groups, or even with the seniors themselves. Volunteers from the farmers' market may be able to help them to the door or back to your car, for instance. Perhaps with the funds raised from the table fees, the parking lot could get modified so that seniors could still park near the front doors without interrupting the rest of the market. It might reduce space available to be used for the farmers' market tables, but after all, the seniors are also members of the community, and the centre should be available for all within it.

 

    Farmers' market's have another added bonus of being better for the environment then grocery stores. The produce sold at a farmers' market has a reduced carbon footprint over that sold in grocery stores. Think about it, the fruits and vegetables in a supermarket have likely been imported from another country, coming in on boats, airplanes, and truck. Whereas the produce found at a farmers' market will have been grown locally, and likely shipped only from the yard it was grown in to the parking lot of the community centre.

 

    My final argument in favour of the farmers' market is health related. Farmers' markets provide fresh seasonal produce, which helps to promote healthier eating. I know that personally, I struggle to eat healthily, but the vegetables I get from a farmers' market are fresher and tastier than those from a grocery store. With the variety and seasonal growth of fruits and vegetables, you'll never get bored from eating the same three plants year round, like I do.

 

    Overall, I fully believe that a Saturday farmer's market will improve the community's health, economy, environment, and bring us all a little bit closer together.

 

    Regards,

        Randy Siemens

Age group 18-39: Yes, in favour.

Age group 40-55: No, not in favour. 

Management: 89% in favour.

Custodial: 98% in favour.

Admin: 42% in favour.

The total cost to the employee would be approximately $129.80 - $139.80 for a set. It could potentially save us money as well, as business attire can be quite expensive and the cost of a uniform set is very fair. 

I understand some of us might be upset that our individuality is stiffened, but I don't believe the office is the place to express yourself. I think there are other ways to express your individuality, not just your clothes.

Thank you for considering my perspective. I look forward to hearing the outcome,

 

Shaelyn LaVacca

Good afternoon, Ms. Smith,

 

Thank you for your proposal to implement a work uniform policy. As you know, we have conducted research, reviewed the pricing of uniforms, and sent out a survey to staff to provide management with appropriate feedback. At this time, I do not believe that the company should move forward with a non-managerial work uniform policy. 

 

I would like to first highlight the results of the employee poll. The management team, who would not be enforced to adhere to the work uniform policy, was largely in favour of the implementation and roll-out of the policy. Given that management would not have to participate in the policy, I do not feel that their poll numbers represent how the majority of the employees feel regarding this proposed policy. Since the purpose of this poll was to gather information on how employees felt, I have based my opinion on those who would be impacted by the policy. Forty-eight percent (48%) of administrative staff and fifty-eight (58%) of contractors were against the implementation of this policy. These results showcase that approximately fifty-three percent (53%) of these combined employees are against the idea. 

 

Custodial staff were largely in favour of the work uniform implementation, with ninety-eight percent (98%) of staff on board. I believe that the custodial staff are in favour of the uniform as their job requirements involve using cleaners, sweeping and mopping, and being around dust and other particles. This environment may cause wear and tear on their personal clothing. While I believe that a non-managerial work uniform policy is not the right direction, it would be worth considering implementing this policy for custodial staff. 

 

Research shows that having the ability to choose the type of clothing one wears improves workplace culture. Employees may be uncomfortable having to follow a strict uniform policy that does not allow for personal expression, or fit with their style preferences. While I can appreciate that a standard uniform may create a more professional work environment, the polls show that non-managerial employees are not fully on board, with the exception of the custodial staff. Perhaps considering more stype options would improve employee polls. 

 

Finally, I would like to address the cost of the uniform, which may be a factor in the low approval ratings. To summarize, I do not believe that a company-wide non-managerial implementation of the work uniform policy should be approved; however, if changes were made to the number of uniforms provided by the company, the selection of styles that were available, and annual replacements provided, it might be worth surveying the employees again to see how they feel about the work uniform policy.

Melissa Mullins

To <MANAGER>

RE: Subject URGENT Mandatory Tipping

 

Dear Mr. Manager,

 

I'm writing to give my personal feedback regarding the proposed mandatory 18% tip added to customer bills at Cozy Corner Bistro. I have had the pleasure of being employed by your establishment as a server since 2018. During my time here, I have had the opportunity to engage with thousands of customers; some young, some old, regulars, shift workers, families, friends, and sometimes individuals who are just passing by. While mandatory tips would be a convenient way to determine and predict income for our employees, it is my opinion that the proposed new policy of mandatory tips added to customer bills would be detrimental change that could ultimately have negative consequences on the business. 

 

    With the ever rising cost of inflation and "tipping fatigue" that all Canadians are facing, some customers may not be able to afford an 18% tip on each of their bills. We have many customers who come in weekly for a coffee break or lunch. These include students, shift workers, seniors on limited pension, and young families with strapped funds. Our tipping model shows that, on average, nearly 50% of our customers generously tip between 15-20% already. The customers who are unable to afford the mandatory 18% tip added to their bill may no longer be able, or willing, to support our bistro, resulting in an overall decline in business and revenue. 

 

    Additionally, I worry that having a required and expected tip added to each bill would have implications on staff performance. Cozy Corner Bistro has a reputation for being friendly, open, warm, and welcoming while serving exceptional food. This change could decrease the incentive for staff to perform superb service at all times to all customers. Customer tips should always be earned, appreciated, but never expected.  

 

    Ultimately, the main concern is that a fair wage should be considered for all of our staff. Our employees should all be given rotating shifts to allow for all to work during peak busy periods to all share in the generosity of our customers that are able to tip according to their personal means. With the cost of living on the rise, it should not land on the customer's wallets to make up for staff low wages while paying a premium on the service they have come to know and expect from our establishment. 

 

In conclusion, I do not think mandatory tipping should be an enforced policy at Cozy Corner Bistro. There is a high risk of a decline in customer business with the proposed new business model, and it should never be an expectation on our clients to have to tip more than they are able to. 

 

I truly appreciate you taking the time to consult with staff regarding this matter. 

 

Best Regards,

Rachel Reid

Server Extraordinaire Since 2023

Dear Management,

 

I've taken notice of the proposal for a standardized workplace uniform. While I do acknowledge some benefits, I believe that overall, this would be a net-negative dress code to implement. 

 

To begin with, I want to address the User Poll relevant to this change, specifically in relation to the difference of approval from different positions. As a contractor, I very much value the individuality of personal wardrobe selection. When interacting with customers, we tend to convey ourselves informally and gain friendly trust as a way of conducting our work. With employees, especially within our department, we enjoy our casual interaction, and it's important to be able to recognize each other from a distance when working in crowds or larger areas. Both of these interactions would be weakened by a standardized outfit; customers would see us more formally and therefore, more faceless and unfriendly, and us contractors would blend in with crowds more often and lose out on personal connection through outfits, which would all hamper our productivity. I believe this explains the discrepancy between our polling and other department's numbers. Custodians work independently and don't interact with customers that often, and management won't be affected by this implementation. Administration could harbour similar grievances to us (given that their polling is similar to ours), but would likely find more value in looking formal to patrons. I would recommend looking into options to implement this uniform on a per-department basis rather than across the whole company.

 

For my other concern, I believe the rollout of the uniform is unfair and costly to employees. One pair of pants and a shirt is unfortunately not sufficient to work with in a 5-day work week. With only one outfit, we would need to wash our clothes every single day, and for a lot of this that is very inconvenient for our circumstances. Some of us live in apartments where laundry is communal, which is a hassle to go through every day, and others may live in areas where the cost of running a washing machine and dryer every single day would really just be taking a hit to our salary. I would please ask that you consider looking into a more nuanced implementation of this outfit, and directly contact representatives from each department to gather a greater picture of your employee wants. Furthermore, regardless of the outcome of those decisions, I would like to see a more generous offer on replacement outfits, or at least more outfits provided to each employee without cost. 

 

Best Regards,

Contractor Connor

Dear Council Members,

 

  I write to you in connection with the recent proposal to build a ring road around our city. I understand many have put pressure on the government to better deal with increased traffic in recent years. However, after careful consideration, I would like to petition that you reject the current proposal. The reason for my position is split into 3 important camps: the land, the cost, and the losers. Please take note of the ill effects this proposal will have on each one. 

 

The Land

 For as long as it has existed, our city has enjoyed an abundance of fresh water, beautiful wildlife, as well as plentiful harvests from the surrounding fields. This has lead to a wonderful city to live in for people of all types. All of which can be directly attributed to the wetlands conservation area. It's untouched and natural ecosystems guard the insects, animals, and watershed needed for the entire region to thrive. 

 The proposed ring road puts the future of that beautiful ecosystem in peril. True, it is only a portion of the wetlands that would be directly paved over. However, the unknown domino effect of removing the homes of a number of the wetlands residents is too big of a risk. Additionally, the increased traffic going right through the centre of that beautiful area will only add to the damage in the future. 

 

The Cost

  As a small but thriving city, we enjoy many wonderful programs and facilities that have become the heart of our community. The recreation centre, library, and public park put on programs nearly every day of the week. These programs bring together our young and our old, uniting us as one city and providing lasting friendships. Those who participate often express how they are proud of what we have built. 

  The proposed ring road will cost the city that pride. The budget pulls money from programs across the city that are the very essence of what it means to live here. All to build a road that’s stated purpose is keeping people away from the heart of the city. That is too big of a cost to justify. 

 

The Losers

  Main street is more than just another road in our city. It is one small portion of a highway between two important places in the province. Every year, a great number of people passing through the city stop. At times for need of refreshments at the convenience store, for food at Mom and Pop Café, or (on a hot summer day) an ice cream in the park. Thousands of dollars are made each year by local businesses, all due to these highway travellers. 

  The proposed ring road will result in significant lost business. Mom and Pop will lose the hungry family wanting a break from the highway. The convenience store will lose all those who need a quick top up of supplies as they rush past. Lost will be the young tourists enjoying an Ice cream in the park as they make their way through the countryside. Due to the lost income, the entire city could end up being "losers" of our favourite places to visit down town. 

 

 It is true, many cities in the province are feeling the effects of increased traffic. However, our city can not submit to the pressure this traffic puts on us. We must guard the land that has supported us for generations. We must support our community by continuing to fund local programs. Most importantly, we must not abandon our core businesses by sending their customers away.  

 

  Council members of our home city, I strongly request you vote to reject the ring road proposal. 

 

Sincerely, 

Tyler Holland

This will greatly affect the best servers working at the Cozy Corner Bistro.

 

If the customers are less inclined to tip over 18% then the servers currently providing the highest quality service will be less inclined to do so, and the servers who were less passionate about the work will then be getting rewarded for putting in less effort than the best of us. Sincerely, 

-Devin

I hope I've convinced you of at least some of my points, or at least brought to light some issues regarding the proposed lane. I thank you for your time and regard, and I hope to hear back from you.

I am writing to make comment on the newly proposed bike only section of main street. Let me first start with, I am an avid proponent of bike lanes and bike access. They are healthy ways of commuting, not just for the cyclists, but for the environment and general health of the inhabitants of a city. This proposed bike lane would not only increase rider safety, but many studies have shown that increased bike and pedestrian access on commercial areas has an outsized benefit to the local economy. This is evident from many examples of pedestrian only and bike/pedestrian only commercial roads.

 

However, I do take issue with the funding and construction proposal of this change. A bike lane may require extensive changes to existing infrastructure, however, changing a street to bike and pedestrian only, requires only that the street be cordoned off, perhaps with bollards, or posts. A 10% increase to business and property taxes seems outsized compared to the work. Additionally, a bike lane sees far less heavy traffic, and thus requires less overall maintenance than a typical heavy traffic street would.

 

Take Mount Royal Avenue in Montreal, QC, which gets closed to heavy vehicle traffic each summer. No such extensive budget goes into this change each year, simply some temporary large decorative concrete balls, planters and other objects, are put in the way, and signs raised to inform drivers of the closure.

 

Similarly, one of the main streets in Victoria, BC also closes during summer to great success, not just for the people who enjoy the city, but the businesses, who see much increased foot traffic and higher sales.

 

This might also be a consideration for the bike only road of our city. That is to say, a temporary closure for the spring to fall, with a reopening in the winter, when fewer cyclists are on the roads and more people wish to drive up close to the businesses they visit as it gets colder.

Best regards,

Ryan Anderson

    Recently, the community has been abuzz with the proposal put forward for the community centre to host a weekly farmers' market in the parking lot. This proposal excites me, but in the community there has been much debate regarding it. The farmers' market, if approved, will interfere with events already held on Saturdays, and some people have concerns about the prices of the wares sold there. I want to put forth an argument in favour of the farmers' market, because I believe that the benefits outweigh the downsides, and I think that a solution can be found that satisfies all parties. 

    Firstly, the proposed farmers' market is a community event, which serves the purpose of the community centre. Vendors can chat with customers while informing them about their wares or produce. Friends can meet and families can enjoy a lovely time examining all the intriguing stands. Farmers' markets support local farmers and entrepreneurs, helping to make Canada a more self-sufficient nation, which is more important than ever in today's volatile global market. The farmer's market also gives those who live in the city access to fresh, high quality produce. Farmers' markets also foster an intermingling of farmers and consumers. This leads farmers to be more in touch with the people that support them and brings consumers to a better understanding of where their food comes from and how it is produced. 

    There have been many valid oppositions raised, however. Some people rightly argue that allowing a weekly farmer's market would interfere with community centre events which are already hosted on Saturdays. Concerns about price of produce have been justly voiced as well. Even though the farmers' market is community event, it pretty much rules out every other possible event at the community centre on Saturdays, as most of the street parking will be presumably used by people shopping at the market. To address these concerns, I have two propositions to put forward. 

    One potential option would be to only allow the farmer's market to run from 7:00 in the morning to noon. This time frame is very common and still allows ample time for shopping. If this idea were implemented, it would free up the community centre parking lot from 12:30 (vendors will need some time to pack up their stands) onwards. 

    Another solution would be to allow the farmer's market to run from 7:00 AM to 7:00 PM, but only at half capacity. There is no need for the farmer's market to have 100 vendors. If a certain portion of the parking lot were reserved for those using the community centre, then people using the community centre on Saturdays would not have to worry as much about parking. OR
Write a letter or an email to city council that clearly explains why you AGREE or DISAGREE with the proposal to replace the existing public park with an 18-hole golf course.
response_text:
RE: Mandatory Lunch Break

 

I would like to begin this e-mail by saying I do, in fact, support the proposal for mandatory lunch breaks; however, my prompt for writing this is the distinct lack of discussion on a few key issues that I believe need to be addressed before we implement this recent (and, admittedly, sudden) proposal.

 

The most prominent concern of those who would otherwise support this proposal seems to be the inflexibility of the time-slot given. In my conversations with co-workers, I've spoken to several who simply cannot adjust their workflow to accommodate a one-hour gap in middle of the day. Their specialized tasks are time-sensitive, with few or no co-workers able to switch out with them during the given time. Many people here simultaneously dread the idea of extending our workday by another hour.

To address these concerns, I'd like to remind everybody that we already make allowances in scheduling for those with unremitting commitments both during and after work. Several persons begin work early and leave early, or vice versa; similarly, the mandatory lunch hour can (and should!) be adjusted to fit the schedule of the individual worker. To add a personal suggestion here: I believe it would serve us well to time the lunch hour of the office and the warehouse to be sequential, rather than simultaneous -- which is a solution my previous workplace took to ensure our break room facilities were never crowded.

 

Another serious issue raised by some of our most hard-working employees is that the company will lose an average of two-hundred-forty work hours, per employee, per year, unless we remain at work an extra hour every day; naturally, this feeds into the first concern. There are two very sensible ways to address this issue. The first is to recognize that we're already a very efficient company. I would like to point out that this is what prompted management to consider this mandatory lunch break in the first place. Barring the busy season (the three months prior to Christmas), many of us have the opportunity to work at a leisurely pace. We all hate to admit it, but there's plenty of time where we really don't have anything to do. Of the above-mentioned two-hundred-forty lost work hours per employee, per year, I believe only a third of those hours are spent on something productive. Don't let this demoralize you: industry-leading examples in Europe (Volkswagen, Dassault Systèmes, or Lufthansa to name a few) started the trend of the seven-hour work day -- with a paid hour for lunch -- almost thirty years ago. Many international companies are learning to reward high standards and exceptional productivity with fantastic benefits, bonuses, and paid time away from work, rather than more work.

Secondly, I would like to remind everybody of last Thursday's tailgate meeting, where Mr. Smith requested that we forward our hiring adverts to qualified friends, family, and acquaintances. We all know the company is still hiring, and having personally spoken to management, I can confirm that the next round of new hires are being taken on with the explicit intent to address the predicted loss of productivity when / if this otherwise extremely popular proposal gains approval.

 

Finally, the claim that this mandatory hour-long break, in combination with our two coffee breaks, will generally create a lazy workplace culture aught to be stopped in its tracks. Despite this idea generally originating with some of our more 'traditional' workers, no evidence and little anecdote has been given to support these claims, which generally work to shame greenhorns into working through their breaks. This is an extremely toxic aspect of workplace culture that is being directly addressed by making the break mandatory. If there wasn't a strong downwards pressure to have people work when they need to pace themselves, we wouldn't need to make this mandatory. The value of pacing your schedule appropriately is well understood by those who have had to deal with the stress of a heavy workload over the holiday season, which need not be extended to all parts of the year by an archaic idea of what constitutes 'Hard Work'. Need I not remind the reader of the astounding boost to productivity early Danish and American industrialists (such as Henry Ford) gained when they introduced the first coffee breaks? The numbers speak for themselves.

 

In conclusion, it is important to remember that the current proposal is simply that: a proposal. It is extremely important the all employees bring their varying views to management so that we can find a solution that both rewards us all for our stellar performance improvements over that last four years, without getting in the way of the special needs of any one worker. We can't work around concerns or scheduling issues if they aren't discussed.

 

Thank you,

 

John Doe, Finance Dept.

email@address.ca | #123-456-7890

Dear Manager,

    A stable source of consistent tips is greater than inconsistent and varied tips. In this email, I will outline three reasons why you should implement this policy to have mandatory 18% tips.

    To begin with, not everybody has the right personality to get high tips. High tips come with good customer service, this is known. However, good customer service is more than nice exchanges at the side of a customer's table. For example, an outgoing server who makes witty jokes with a customer can scribble their order onto their notepad and haphazardly leave it at the chef's side. This could open up the possibility of the chef misreading the note and missing a part of the customer's order, wasting both the restaurant's good reputation, time, and money. Contrarily, an introverted server could stutter while taking the order, then walk it over to the chef, explaining it in perfect detail, and ensuring the order was made right. If both meals were made correctly, regardless of the attention to detail, I'm sure the outgoing server would get a higher tip. Mandatory tips ensure that people are given a stable base-line pay despite how their differences.

    Continuing on, mandatory tips means there is less stress on the workers to perform. I believe that the reduced stress would ensure fewer accidents in the workplace, and greater customer service. For example, if a server needed extra money for an emergency, for example, to replace the head-lights on their car, they would be pressured to move quickly and get a large tip. This could result in them dropping a dish or writing an order wrong, resulting in a loss for the restaurant, and the server in the end. They could even potentially injure themselves or a customer. By implementing mandatory tips, servers would have less stress, and a higher base-line rate, which stops them from worrying about variable tips impacting their ability to handle an emergency, letting them focus on the customer's needs.

    Finally, an 18% tip is greater than the average tip, along with the fact that customers are increasingly choosing to not tip at all. Nearly half of all customers tip either 10% or 15%, with the next highest being 20%. By setting the mandatory tip to 18%, not only are server's getting greater tips on average, but they're getting tips that never would have been there, from customers that would have refused to tip.

    In conclusion, the mandatory 18% tip provides a stable base-line that improves the average pay of the restaurant's servers, reduces their stress, letting them focus entirely on the customer, and eliminates the inequality between servers who have a preferable personality for serving and those that have a less preferable one. It is for these reasons that I am entirely in support of implementing the mandatory 18% tip policy.

 

Sincerely, an employee

Dear Manager, 

Recently we were asked to share our opinion on the proposed mandatory social fund. I understand the intent of this initiative, however in my opinion this is not the most meaningful way to support the staff or boost morale. 

In the current economy, the cost of living continues to increase relentlessly and more people than ever are living paycheque to paycheque. Mandating participation may not only be a financial burden to some but may also result in a negative experience for an employee.  Those struggling financially may face undue hardship, embarrassment, or it may cause them to isolate themselves from the rest of the team which is the opposite of what the program is trying to achieve.

Finances aside, there is also a variance around the level of interest. There is higher interest in the team members that are under 40 years old, possibly because they have a greater desire to socialize with their peers and are more motivated by "perks" than their older teammates. The older generations typically have expectations of coming to work to do their jobs with no fanfare or frills, and their reward is their paycheque. Since this division is based on the different age groups it could cause additional division within the teams.

Another area I feel may cause friction would be the use of the funds. Potential questions like "Who would make the decisions on how to use the money?" "How will we know how the money is being spent?" and "What if the employee doesn't like the gift they received?" Additionally, not everyone wants to be celebrated for a wedding, the birth of a child, or their retirement and others may not have any of those major life events to celebrate. If the decision is to use the funds for parties, snacks, or coffee stations, equal options would need to be available to all employees regardless of any personal dietary requirements (allergies, religious requirements, etc.) for it to remain inclusive or there is the risk of alienating the employees that cannot participate after they were forced to contribute. 

My main concern is that it may segregate people instead of bringing them together and cause resentment instead of appreciation which is why I do not agree with the mandatory social fund. 

I appreciate what the company is trying to achieve, and I would love to help find other options we can use to drive staff morale, job satisfaction, and ultimately reduce turnover. 

Respectfully, 

Tracey Yorke

For as long as the monetary system we have in place today, workplace standards in regard to workers health and safety have been disputed. It is crucial that the voice of every worker and their personal opinion are taking into consideration within line with the possible changes made to lunch break time. It is reasonable to assume a mandatory 1-hour lunch break is of upmost priority to the workers and the company.

 

    Primarily, when employees are given sufficient time to eat lunch, will have a direct interplay with productivity, group moral, and overall efficiency. Eating a balanced diet and given time to allow those nutrients to digest increases energy and heightens mood in a positive way, which will have a direct impact on the output of the workforce. With this being said it's at our discourse to realize the impact this has on health, safety, and the workplace dynamic.

 

    Additionally, given people have the necessary time to socialize and rest is a fundamental way to bring the workplace together. By doing so increases team work, allows time to problem-solve crucial implications during working time, and can allow the mind and body to step away from rational thinking. Which acts as a way to relief stress, increase creativity, and disconnect from things they can not resolve on a moments notice while on shift time. This is in itself a part of all aspects of life no just time spent at work.

 

    Conversely, critiques might argue that taking 1 hour lunch takes away from the total time spend on production, which in turn reduces monetary gain. However, the brain has a limitation to output based on how it has evolved over the course of human existence. Natural maximum output for any sport, strength training, learning complex tasks, or creating is limited to 3–4 hours at peak effectiveness and slowly declines thereafter. At which point fatigue sets in and mistakes, problems and incidents arise. So it is obvious that trying to add more work time doesn't always procure a more productive and safer workforce. 

 

In conclusion, it is absolutely imperative the topics discussed are taking into consideration before final decisions are made to effect the workplace as a whole. At the liberty of people, and what we value together, it is possible to draw a reasonable resolution. To meet the needs of the workplace and its people that make possible, a safe and healthy environment. In effect the very act of retaining a baseline or neutral position of rest, play and nourishment. David Michael O'Neill

Monday, August 31, 2026
 

Dear Home style Inc,  

 

My name is Phil, I have been an employee with the company for a few years now. I'm writing this letter regarding the companies proposal to have a mandatory social fund. I have to disagree with this proposal. My main reason for disagreeing with this proposal is because it doesn't seem fair to me that there will be a mandatory $100 contribution yearly. Through our online chat portal JR15 says "I can barely afford to buy gifts for my own family." This is true for many of us who are paycheck to paycheck. Employees don't want to be forced to spend our money on company events. This should be covered by the company as a sign of gratitude for our hard work. 

 

    I think having social company events is a good idea, but don't think it should be mandatory for employees to have to dish out from their paycheck. This takes the fun out of it for some people. Some of us have families we would rather spend our hard-earned money on. I don't want the company wasting my money on parties that we are being forced to go to. According to Connecting Careers User Poll, the majority of people who believe social funds boost staff moral are the youngest age group. People between the age of 18-24. Not all of them, but 79% of the people in this age group fell it will boost moral. On the other-side of the spectrum, 73% of people 55+ don't feel it will boost staff moral. There has to be a better way to get staff together and make everyone want to be included. 

 

    The social fund wants employees money to go towards parties, gifts, flowers and a coffee station. These are all things the company should be providing. Seems a bit disappointing the company would take money from the staff to provide this. I read in a blog, Modern Workplace Trends with the title Boosting Staff Morale. That a number of surveys show that staff morale is important to job satisfaction. I believe this to be true, however there are other ways employers can have aside social funds, Like having a fund-raiser. 

 

    It was my experience with my previous company that the cost of company events were covered by the employers. This just makes the most sense to me. Everyone would show up to social events like Christmas parties, and there was little to no pressure on the staff. By the company covering the cost of these events it made me as an employee fell thought of and respected. By having a mandatory social fund I personally would feel forced to be part in social events, and it's not as welcoming to newer employees.  

 

    In conclusion, I disagree with the proposal to have a mandatory social fund. Being forced to pay for company social events just feels wrong to me. We don't need fancy parties with gifts and flowers to have a good time at a social event. I would be happier having a bowling night, or outdoor BBQ. I also don't want the company going out-of-pocket spending money needlessly. Let's keep it simple and cost-effective to enjoy the company of staff and employers at social events. We should have a company meeting to explore other options. 

 

Respectfully, 

 

Phil
